Assets.Functionality: Top-level input that signals a machine software interrupt; combined with other machine interrupts and forwarded to the control unit as part of the machine interrupt vector.
Assets.Justification: This external interrupt input can be asserted from integration to forcibly interrupt or repeatedly trigger the CPU, which can prevent forward progress or starve normal execution (DoS). It does not carry secret data and primarily impacts CPU liveness, so availability is the dominant objective.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level input that signals an external machine interrupt; combined into the machine interrupt vector and handled by the control unit.
Assets.Justification: An attacker-controllable external interrupt line can be used to repeatedly interrupt or preempt CPU operation, denying normal service and causing availability loss. It affects control flow and liveness rather than confidentiality, making availability the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Signals alignment or access error conditions reported by the LSU for memory operations.
Assets.Justification: lsu_err is used to detect and handle erroneous memory accesses; if these error signals are falsified or suppressed, errors may be masked leading to silent data corruption or security policy bypass. Integrity of error reporting is required to maintain correct error handling and memory safety.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level input that signals a machine timer interrupt; combined into the machine interrupt vector and used by the control unit to trigger timer handling.
Assets.Justification: Manipulation of the timer interrupt can force excessive interrupt handling or prevent progress (timing-based DoS), directly impacting CPU availability. It is an externally observable control input without secret data content.

Assets.Functionality: 16-bit vector of custom fast interrupts supplied to the control unit as irq_fast_i for low-latency interrupt handling.
Assets.Justification: Because multiple fast interrupt sources can be asserted at integration level, an attacker can flood or permanently assert these lines to preempt normal execution and cause denial of service; the vector primarily affects liveness rather than data secrecy.

Assets.Functionality: Debug/halt request input presented to the control unit (irq_dbg_i) to enter, halt, or manage debug mode and parking loops.
Assets.Justification: Asserting this input can park or halt the CPU, stopping normal operation entirely and enabling a straightforward DoS at integration level; it is a control input that affects operational availability rather than confidentiality.

Assets.Functionality: External signal that indicates completion of a memory synchronization operation; forwarded to the control unit to resume dependent operations.
Assets.Justification: If this synchronization completion input is not asserted or is tampered with, the CPU may remain stalled waiting for completion and thus block progress (availability impact). It does not contain secret data and primarily gates operation resumption.

Assets.Functionality: Primary ALU result vector produced by arithmetic/logic operations; selected as register-file write-back data for instruction results.
Assets.Justification: alu_res is the value committed to the architectural state; any corruption or mis-selection propagates wrong data into the register file, leading to incorrect control-flow targets, miscomputed addresses, and silent state corruption—violating ISA correctness.

Assets.Functionality: Address/addition result from the ALU used for memory address computation and forwarded to the LSU and PMP for load/store accesses and permission checks.
Assets.Justification: alu_add directly determines memory access targets; corruption or unintended modification of this value results in incorrect memory reads/writes and potential data corruption or privilege bypass. Therefore integrity of this signal is critical to correct CPU behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Data returned from the load/store unit after a memory read; can be selected for write-back into the register file or forwarded to other units.
Assets.Justification: lsu_rdata supplies data from memory into the CPU; if this signal is corrupted (e.g., via integration-level manipulation of the memory interface), it will corrupt register contents and program behavior, so integrity protection is required.

Assets.Functionality: Memory Address Register from the LSU that reflects the current memory access address; provided to control and PMP for diagnostics and checks.
Assets.Justification: lsu_mar carries the effective address used for PMP checks and for indexing memory; if corrupted, loads/stores are directed to the wrong location or protection is mis-evaluated, enabling silent data corruption or unauthorized access.

Assets.Functionality: Flow-control signal driven by the LSU to indicate that a data-bus access is still outstanding and that the pipeline/back-end must stall or wait.
Assets.Justification: If lsu_wait is asserted incorrectly or held asserted, the backend will stall and the CPU cannot make forward progress, enabling a denial-of-service at the integration level; this is primarily an availability issue.

Assets.Functionality: Flag indicating a PMP permission violation reported by the PMP unit; forwarded to the control unit to trigger access faults or prevent operations.
Assets.Justification: An asserted pmp_fault will prevent or abort memory accesses and trigger exception handling, potentially preventing normal operation; at integration level forcing such faults results mainly in availability impact (blocked accesses).

Assets.Functionality: CSR read data produced/forwarded by the control unit; selectable for write-back into the register file and used for configuration/status decisions.
Assets.Justification: csr_rdata contains control/status values read from CSRs; if this is altered, registers and subsequent operations may be loaded with incorrect configuration or status values, corrupting system behavior (integrity).

Assets.Functionality: Register-file source operand 1 used across the ALU: comparator, adder/subtractor, bit-manipulation, shifter, mul/div, FPU, CFU and other co-processors as an input operand.
Assets.Justification: If rs1_i is modified at integration (e.g., by a bus fault or malicious connection), ALU and co-processor computations will produce incorrect results, corrupting program state and memory accesses. The operand's integrity directly affects correctness of addresses, comparisons and any operation that consumes rs1_i.

Assets.Functionality: Register-file source operand 2 selected as ALU second operand or used by co-processors (mul/div, bitmanip, crypto, etc.) and for shift amount extraction.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of rs2_i can change arithmetic results, shift amounts and addresses, leading to wrong memory accesses or control/data corruption. Because many ALU operations and co-processors rely on this value, its integrity is critical to correct CPU behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Register-file source operand 3 provided to units that require a third operand such as the FPU and CFU (custom functions unit).
Assets.Justification: When used, rs3_i is an essential operand for multi-operand instructions/co-processors; tampering with it changes co-processor results and may corrupt computation or cryptographic operations. Its integrity is required to ensure correctness of any instruction relying on three operands.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit comparator status reporting equality and less-than results used for branch/conditional decisions and by co-processors.
Assets.Justification: Altering comparator outputs causes incorrect branch decisions and control-flow changes, which can lead to incorrect program execution or privilege escalation. The comparator bits directly influence control-flow decisions, so their integrity is dominant.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit primary ALU output that presents the selected ALU or co-processor result to the rest of the CPU for writeback/next-stage usage.
Assets.Justification: res_o is the main data output of the ALU; if it is corrupted or forged, the CPU will write incorrect data into the register file or memory, compromising program correctness and system integrity. Protecting the integrity of computation results is therefore critical.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit direct adder/subtractor output used for address generation and explicit adder results.
Assets.Justification: A corrupted add_o will result in incorrect memory addresses, causing wrong reads/writes and potential security/stability failures (data corruption or unintended access). Because addresses determine what memory is accessed, integrity of add_o is vital.

Assets.Functionality: Result produced by the CFU (custom functions unit) which may be forwarded into cp_result(4) and then to cp_res/res_o when CFU operations are active.
Assets.Justification: cfu_res is an input to the aggregated co-processor result path; manipulation of this signal can produce arbitrary ALU outputs under custom instruction execution. Protecting it prevents malicious or erroneous CFU outputs from impacting the CPU state.

Assets.Functionality: Aggregated CSR read data routed from co-processor CSR proxies (FPU/CFU) to the CPU CSR read interface.
Assets.Justification: csr_o can expose internal configuration or status registers (FPU/CFU CSRs). If CSR contents are sensitive (debug info, status, or custom-unit secrets), uncontrolled exposure via csr_o is a confidentiality risk; therefore confidentiality is the dominant concern for the CSR read-back path.

Assets.Functionality: Strobe asserted when any multi-cycle co-processor indicates a valid result, signaling the CPU that a co-processor result is/ will be available.
Assets.Justification: If done_o is prevented from asserting (or spuriously asserted) at integration level, the CPU may stall waiting for results or proceed incorrectly, causing denial-of-service or lost/coherency errors. Availability of the completion signal is therefore critical to co-processor operation.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN+1-bit adder/subtractor result (includes carry/borrow) used for add/sub results, address output and to derive slt flags.
Assets.Justification: addsub_res feeds address outputs, SLT status, and the add result; tampering with it will change addresses, comparisons and arithmetic results, directly compromising correctness of memory and control decisions.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit vector formed by ORing individual co-processor outputs; selected as ALU result when a co-processor operation is active.
Assets.Justification: cp_res drives res_o when co-processors are active; if cp_res is corrupted, co-processor outputs (including any cryptographic or numerical results) will be wrong and propagate to the CPU state, harming integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Vector of valid/done flags (one per co-processor) indicating that a co-processor will produce its result in the next cycle; used to assert done_o and to time multi-cycle outputs.
Assets.Justification: If cp_valid signals are blocked or stuck, done_o will not assert and multi-cycle co-processor operations will appear unavailable to the CPU, causing hangs or denial-of-service. Thus availability of valid strobes is the main concern.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates a physical memory protection (PMP) execute/fetch fault and is forwarded into the trap logic to mark an instruction fetch bus error (trap_ctrl.instr_be) that can trigger synchronous exceptions during instruction execution.
Assets.Justification: pmp_fault_i gates exception entry on illegal fetches; spurious assertion causes repeated trap entry (exception storms) that prevent forward progress, while suppression on real faults leads to endless failing fetches or hangs in non-responding regions—both directly degrading availability.

Assets.Functionality: External input request that triggers a debug/halt entry (used to stop the CPU into debug mode).
Assets.Justification: Asserting this input will stop normal CPU execution by requesting a debug halt; a malicious or faulty assertion can deny service by permanently halting or repeatedly suspending execution. Protecting this input prevents obvious denial-of-service at integration level.

Assets.Functionality: Load/store unit wait flag indicating that a memory transaction is pending; the execute FSM stalls on this signal while waiting for memory responses.
Assets.Justification: Forcing or holding this signal can stall the EXEC engine waiting for memory responses and thereby cause prolonged blocking or denial-of-service of instruction progress. Protecting against malicious or stuck assertions prevents DoS at integration level.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates completion of memory synchronization/fence operations; used to progress FENCE handling and to update exe_engine.msync.
Assets.Justification: If this input is prevented from asserting or spoofed, fence/fence.i operations may be blocked or mis-ordered, causing the CPU to stall or execute incorrect memory-order semantics; this can be exploited to produce denial-of-service or correctness failures, so availability is primary.

Assets.Functionality: Handshake/status from a multi-cycle ALU co-processor indicating operation completion so the control FSM can continue and perform write-back.
Assets.Justification: alu_cp_done_i advances the pipeline from a multi-cycle op; if suppressed, the FSM never leaves the busy state and forward progress stalls, while spurious assertion retires incomplete results and can force replays or exception loops—both degrade system availability.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit vector indicating load/store alignment and access errors used to populate synchronous exception buffer bits and trigger traps.
Assets.Justification: Falsely asserting errors will generate exceptions/traps and change saved PC/CSR state (mtval, mepc, mcause), corrupting program flow and state. Integrity of these error indicators is needed to avoid spurious or malicious trap generation.

Assets.Functionality: Synchronous exception buffer (bit-per-exception) that latches synchronous exceptions until they are handled and is used to select trap cause.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of exception buffer bits can hide or inject synchronous exceptions, altering which trap gets delivered and potentially changing saved context (mepc/mtval/mcause). Ensuring integrity prevents unauthorized or spurious exception handling.

Assets.Functionality: Defines the conditions under which a CSR update is performed. The logic uses csr.we and related checks, such as illegal instruction and privilege validation, to gate register writes.
Assets.Justification: If these control signals are compromised, privileged CSRs could be inappropriately modified or blocked, disrupting configuration and control flow. Ensuring the integrity of csr.we prevents unauthorized or erroneous updates to critical registers.

Assets.Functionality: Masked/latched interrupt buffer that holds asynchronous interrupt requests, respects masking and env_pending semantics and is used for prioritization.
Assets.Justification: irq_buf preserves and masks asynchronous requests until servicing; if it fails to latch or is cleared spuriously, genuine interrupts are lost and time-critical service is delayed, while if stuck asserted it can trigger interrupt storms that monopolize execution—both conditions impede forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag indicating the CPU is in debug-mode (online). It changes privilege/behavior and how traps/CSRs are accessed.
Assets.Justification: Improper setting of debug mode can deny normal operation (stay halted or prevent interrupts) or allow privileged debug operations; its primary risk is denial-of-service or persistent debug state, so availability is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Per-counter increment-enable input that, when asserted, causes the low-word (and via carry the high-word) to increment on the next rising clock edge.
Assets.Justification: inc_i determines when the counter advances; spurious assertion or suppression skews lo_q/hi_q (and cy_q propagation), producing incorrect counts that silently corrupt profiling, timing, or security checks that rely on the counter.

Assets.Functionality: Selects whether the low-word (sel='0') or high-word (sel='1') of a multi-word counter is accessed for read or write operations.
Assets.Justification: sel_i controls which half of the counter is targeted; flipping it causes reads/writes to hit the wrong sub-word (e.g., updating hi_q instead of lo_q), breaking carry semantics and corrupting the aggregate counter value.

Assets.Functionality: Write-enable input that allows wdata_i to be written into the selected low or high sub-word register on the next clock edge.
Assets.Justification: we_i governs whether state is overwritten; unintended assertion clobbers the selected sub-word with arbitrary data, while suppression prevents legitimate updates, both yielding incorrect counter state.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit write-data bus used to load values into the selected low/high sub-word when we_i is asserted.
Assets.Justification: wdata_i is the value committed to lo_q/hi_q when writes occur; corruption injects arbitrary counts or resets, silently altering measurements and invalidating any logic keyed to the counter.

Assets.Functionality: Read-data output of the generic counter returning the selected sub-word (zero-extended to XLEN) to the top-level instantiation for CSR readback aggregation.
Assets.Justification: rdata_o is the reported counter value; if mis-selected or corrupted, software observes a wrong count, leading to faulty decisions and masking underlying tampering with the actual state.

Assets.Functionality: Registers that hold the low-word (lo_q) of the counter; they are the canonical storage of the counter value and are updated by writes, increments and carry logic.
Assets.Justification: lo_q holds the canonical low bits of a hardware counter and can be directly written via CSR low-word writes; unauthorized modification or corruption of lo_q will change the counter value and break correctness of any logic depending on the counter, making it an integrity-critical asset.

Assets.Functionality: Registers that hold the high-word (hi_q) of the counter; they are the canonical storage of the counter value and are updated by writes, increments and carry logic.
Assets.Justification: hi_q forms the upper portion of wide counters and is writable via CSR; tampering or unintended writes to hi_q corrupt the overall counter value (particularly for wide counters), so it must be protected to maintain counter integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 16-bit vector of per-counter increment-enable signals derived each clock from event inputs, cpu_debug and cnt_halt; each bit gates whether its counter increments when its event fires.
Assets.Justification: cnt_en gates whether counters advance; preventing increments (or forcing them stuck at zero) can effectively deny the availability of up-to-date counter values and impair monitoring, scheduling, or any dependent functionality. Thus cnt_en is a dominant availability asset because its disruption impacts the operational usefulness of the counters.

Assets.Functionality: Array of per-HPM 12-bit configuration registers that select which events will increment each hardware performance monitor; updated on cfg writes and used to gate events when computing cnt_en.
Assets.Justification: hpmevent controls which events cause the HPM counters to increment; an unauthorized modification will change the observable performance metrics and corrupt the semantic meaning of HPM counts. Therefore, protecting hpmevent from unauthorized writes is essential to preserve the integrity of performance-monitoring data and any functionality that relies on those counts.

Assets.Functionality: Per-index read strobe generated by combining cnt_acc, sel, and CSR read signals to enable reads from individual counters.
Assets.Justification: cnt_re qualifies which counter and cycle are read; if asserted for the wrong index or suppressed when intended, the mux returns incorrect or stale values, misleading software and masking tampering—thus the correctness of readback depends on its integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Per-index write strobe generated by combining cnt_acc, sel, and CSR write signals to enable writes to individual counters.
Assets.Justification: cnt_we directly enables CSR writes into counter registers; if these enables are manipulated an attacker could inject arbitrary values into counters, corrupting counter state and breaking any logic that relies on correct counts. Thus cnt_we is an integrity-critical control point for counter contents.

Assets.Functionality: Signals that aggregate and present the selected counter or mhpmevent configuration data onto the module's read-data path for CSR read operations.
Assets.Justification: These signals are the final internal representation of what will be returned on reads; corruption or incorrect values here directly yield wrong read-outs to software, violating data correctness (integrity).

Assets.Functionality: Per-index write strobe for mhpmevent configuration CSRs, asserted when cfg_acc, sel, and the CSR write strobe are active.
Assets.Justification: cfg_we authorizes which mhpmevent entry is modified; spurious assertion or wrong-index gating corrupts event selectors and masks/forges measurements, while suppression blocks legitimate updates—compromising the correctness of counter configuration.

Assets.Functionality: Per-index read strobe for mhpmevent configuration CSRs, asserted when cfg_acc, sel, and the CSR read strobe are active.
Assets.Justification: cfg_re qualifies which configuration entry is observed; if mis-asserted or suppressed, software reads the wrong index or stale data, leading to incorrect diagnostics and hiding tampering with the actual mhpmevent settings.

Assets.Functionality: Register-file source operand 1 (XLEN bits) that supplies the primary data input for all bit-manipulation operations (shifts/rotates, logical ops, pack/zip, CLMUL, etc.).
Assets.Justification: rs1_i supplies the principal data consumed by virtually every operation in the unit; any unauthorized modification of this input will directly corrupt computed results. Protecting its integrity is therefore required to prevent incorrect or adversarial outputs from the co-processor.

Assets.Functionality: Register-file source operand 2 (XLEN bits) used as the secondary input for operations that require two operands (e.g., shifted-add, pack, logical ops, carry-less multiplication).
Assets.Justification: rs2_i is used in arithmetic/bit-manipulation operations and in the CLMUL path; any tampering or corruption of this operand will alter results and can subvert correctness or downstream computations. Ensuring integrity prevents malicious or accidental corruption of operations that depend on the second operand.

Assets.Functionality: Shift amount input (index_size_f(XLEN) bits) that controls rotate/shift distance, one-hot position selection for single-bit ops, and initialization of iterative shifter counters.
Assets.Justification: shamt_i directly controls the behavior of shifts/rotates and single-bit operations (BSET/BCLR/BINV/BEXT); if altered, the operation semantics and selected bit positions change, producing incorrect or malicious results. Thus shamt_i integrity is critical to preserve correct control of data transformations.

Assets.Functionality: Comparator status input (2 bits) from the core; one bit (less) is sampled into less_reg and used to select between operands for min/max instructions and similar conditional selections.
Assets.Justification: cmp_i (and the sampled less flag) affects branch-less selection logic such as min/max; corruption of comparator inputs will cause incorrect operand selection and thus incorrect computation. Protecting cmp_i integrity is necessary to avoid maliciously forced selection of data values.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit synchronous result output presenting the computed result of the selected bit-manipulation operation when the internal valid signal indicates completion.
Assets.Justification: res_o is the primary interface by which the CPU obtains computed results; if this output is prevented from being delivered (stuck/blocked) the co-processor cannot supply results to the rest of the system, causing a denial-of-service. Ensuring res_o availability is required for correct operation and service continuity.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit valid output that indicates res_o contains a valid finished result from the co-processor unit (asserted when operations complete or single-cycle ops finish).
Assets.Justification: valid_o gates consumer use of res_o; if the valid flag is suppressed or erroneously deasserted, downstream logic will not consume results and the operation effectively experiences denial-of-service. Protecting availability of valid_o ensures completed results are announced and usable.

Assets.Functionality: One-hot vector of decoded operation commands produced by the instruction decoder that selects which internal operation path (ANDN, ORN, ROT, CLMUL, etc.) to execute.
Assets.Justification: cmd determines which internal functional block is enabled for a given instruction; corruption or manipulation of the decoded command can cause execution of the wrong operation, producing incorrect or malicious outputs. Hence the integrity of the decode vector is critical to maintain correct instruction semantics.

Assets.Functionality: Internal capture/buffer of rs1_i sampled when a co-processor operation is active; used by all internal operations (shifter, logical ops, pack/zip, CLMUL paths).
Assets.Justification: rs1_reg is the internal stored copy of the first operand used across multiple cycles and functional units; tampering with this register corrupts all computations derived from it. Maintaining the integrity of rs1_reg is essential to ensure correct multi-cycle and pipelined operation.

Assets.Functionality: Internal 2*XLEN-bit result register used by the iterative carry-less multiplier core to accumulate intermediate and final multiplication results, later driving the CLMUL output words.
Assets.Justification: clmul.res holds intermediate multiplication state and final product used for res_int(op_clmul_c). Corruption of this register during iteration will produce incorrect multiplication outputs, so maintaining its integrity is necessary for correct arithmetic behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Internal capture/buffer of rs2_i sampled for use in operations requiring a second operand (e.g., SHADD, PACK, CLMUL).
Assets.Justification: rs2_reg holds the second operand used by arithmetic and bitwise functions; corrupting rs2_reg will change results of two-operand operations and can silently subvert computations. Therefore its integrity must be preserved.

Assets.Functionality: Internal shift register inside the shifter unit that holds shifting data and provides the rotate/shift result or iterative intermediate state for bit scans/counts.
Assets.Justification: shifter.sreg directly supplies the rotate/shift output (res_int(op_rot_c)) and is used iteratively for scans and counts; corruption of this register will yield incorrect shift/scan results and can subvert population/count operations. Its integrity is therefore critical to correctness of many bit-manipulation functions.

Assets.Functionality: Array of four 32-bit CFU-internal control/status registers that hold the 128-bit XTEA key material and are read/written via the CFU CSR interface.
Assets.Justification: key_mem holds the cryptographic key material used by the XTEA implementation. Disclosure of its contents (via reads or side-channels) would reveal secret key material and compromise confidentiality of encryption/decryption.

Assets.Asset Name: CSR Read Data Output (CFU CSR read port)
Assets.Functionality: Asynchronous 32-bit output that presents the contents of key_mem[index] (selected by csr_addr_i) to the external CSR read bus.
Assets.Justification: csr_rdata_o exposes key_mem contents to the CPU and thus forms a direct leakage channel for key material; uncontrolled reads or weakened protection of this output leaks confidential key material.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit internal done/shifter that implements the multi-cycle processing latency and directly controls when valid_o is asserted.
Assets.Justification: xtea.done gates valid_o and therefore the visibility of results to the CPU; if xtea.done is corrupted or prevented from progressing, operations will not complete and the unit will effectively be denied (availability impact).

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit source register 1 operand provided by the CPU and captured into xtea.opa for computation.
Assets.Justification: Alteration of rs1_i (injected or corrupted operand) changes the computed result and can cause incorrect encryption/decryption behavior; integrity of operand inputs is required for correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit source register 2 operand provided by the CPU and captured into xtea.opb for computation.
Assets.Justification: rs2_i directly influences the cryptographic computation; unauthorized modification leads to corrupted results, so maintaining integrity of this operand is essential.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit write data presented on CSR writes; when csr_we_i is asserted and csr_addr_i selects a key index, this value is written into key_mem.
Assets.Justification: csr_wdata_i carries values that directly modify the key storage; unauthorized or corrupted write data would change key material and compromise the correctness and trustworthiness of subsequent cryptographic operations.

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle strobe that enables synchronous writes into key_mem at the addressed CSR index when asserted during a rising clock edge.
Assets.Justification: csr_we_i controls whether incoming CSR data is committed to key storage; an attacker that can assert or suppress this signal can inject or prevent key updates, directly compromising key integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit address selecting which of the four key_mem entries (CFU CSRs) is read or written during CSR accesses.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with csr_addr_i could cause writes to land in the wrong key slot or overwrite critical key words, corrupting the stored key and breaking integrity of the cryptographic state.

Assets.Functionality: 3-bit function/immediate field from the custom instruction that selects the CFU operation (XTEA encrypt variant, decrypt variant, init, etc.) and influences internal control and arithmetic.
Assets.Justification: funct3_i determines algorithmic behavior (initialization vs. encrypt/decrypt and operand selection); tampering can change how the key and operands are used, leading to incorrect or maliciously altered cryptographic results.

Assets.Functionality: 1-bit input that selects R3 vs R4 instruction semantics and thereby affects which operands are used and which result paths are selected.
Assets.Justification: rtype_i steers decode semantics and datapath selection; if flipped or glitched, the unit consumes the wrong operand set and returns a mismatched result path, producing incorrect computations and violating architectural correctness.

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle strobe that triggers a CFU operation; when asserted and instruction type matches, the CFU latches operands and begins processing.
Assets.Justification: If start_i is suppressed or blocked, legitimate CFU operations cannot be initiated, causing a denial of service for custom instructions; conversely, spurious asserts could cause unexpected operations, impacting availability of expected service.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates the CPU is waiting for the CFU and gates whether the CFU may continue processing; clearing it should terminate/reset internal operations.
Assets.Justification: active_i gates whether the CFU should continue processing; malicious deassertion during an operation can prematurely stop processing (denial of service) or prevent completion, so availability depends on its correct behavior.

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle output asserted to indicate result_o is valid; the CPU samples this while active_i is high to accept and write back the result to the register file.
Assets.Justification: valid_o informs the CPU that a result is ready; if it is suppressed or stuck, the CPU will not accept the result and operations time out (denial of service), making valid_o availability-critical.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-wide register-file source 1. When a valid conditional co-processor instruction is detected and the evaluated condition is true, rs1_i is forwarded to the operation result res_o.
Assets.Justification: Modification or corruption of rs1_i directly changes the value forwarded to res_o, producing incorrect results in the processor datapath. Protecting the integrity of rs1_i is necessary to prevent unauthorized tampering that would corrupt program state or computations.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-wide register-file source 2. rs2_i is compared against zero to produce rs2_zero, which together with funct3 selects the conditional semantics (equal / not-equal) and thus controls whether rs1_i is forwarded.
Assets.Justification: Altering rs2_i changes rs2_zero and therefore the evaluated condition; this can cause incorrect enabling or suppression of the forwarding path and lead to incorrect control flow or results. Thus the integrity of rs2_i must be preserved to prevent logic corruption of the conditional operation.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-wide operation result driven by the module. When a valid_cmd is asserted and the condition is true, res_o is driven with rs1_i; otherwise res_o is driven with zero. Downstream logic consumes res_o.
Assets.Justification: If res_o is prevented from conveying the produced result (for example forced to zero or otherwise made unavailable), downstream logic cannot receive the operation outcome and the co-processor conditional operation effectively fails, producing a denial-of-service at integration level. Ensuring res_o availability is therefore critical for correct module operation.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit flag indicating that the module detected a valid conditional co-processor instruction (valid_cmd) and thus that res_o is meaningful for the current cycle.
Assets.Justification: If valid_o is suppressed or manipulated so that downstream logic never sees a valid indication, legitimate results may be ignored and the conditional operation cannot be used, causing a denial-of-service at system level. The availability of valid_o is therefore necessary to ensure proper handoff of results to the rest of the processor.

Assets.Functionality: Combinational flag that detects whether the current instruction matches the co-processor conditional operation (derived from ctrl_i fields). It gates the unit operation and is forwarded to valid_o.
Assets.Justification: If valid_cmd is corrupted (wrongly asserted or deasserted), the unit may erroneously execute or skip conditional moves, producing incorrect data movement or control-flow behavior. As the internal selector that enables operation, its correctness directly impacts functional integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Internal 1-bit signal equal to (rs2_zero xnor ctrl_i.ir_funct3(1)); it represents the final boolean condition deciding whether rs1_i will be forwarded on a valid command.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the condition signal (or its inputs) directly changes the decision to forward rs1_i, causing incorrect selection of data flow and corrupting operation outcomes. Protecting the integrity of this internal decision point is essential to prevent faulty or malicious control of forwarding behavior.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit operand source 1 supplied by the CPU register file; used as the primary data input for permutations, hash functions and block-cipher XOR operations.
Assets.Justification: rs1_i may contain plaintexts, key material, or key-dependent intermediates; disclosure via probes, debug, or side channels leaks sensitive information and weakens cryptographic protections.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit operand source 2 from the CPU register file; used for indexing, S-box lookups, rotation select fields and as the second operand for many crypto operations.
Assets.Justification: rs2_i often encodes secret-dependent selectors, indices, or data; observing it reveals patterns correlated with keys or plaintexts, enabling inference attacks, so it must remain confidential.

Assets.Functionality: Registered 8-bit output from the AES S-box lookup (forward or inverse depending on aes.dec) that feeds the MixColumns math and later rounds.
Assets.Justification: The S-box output is a key-dependent intermediate; exposing or correlating this byte facilitates differential/correlation attacks, so it must not be observable outside the crypto core.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered 12-bit instruction field sampled from ctrl_i that configures sub-operation selection, S-box direction, rotation amounts and other functional-unit behaviors.
Assets.Justification: funct12 chooses the crypto sub-operation and internal routing; tampering causes the unit to execute the wrong function or direction (e.g., AES enc/dec), yielding incorrect results and violating architectural correctness.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit block cipher result computed as rs1 xor rol_res; used as the block-cipher operation output and potentially routed to res_o.
Assets.Justification: blk_res is the computed round/output word; corruption here produces wrong ciphertext or intermediates that propagate to res_o, silently compromising cryptographic correctness.

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle internal pulse generated by the controller to indicate processing completion and to enable result routing and valid_o for a single cycle.
Assets.Justification: The one-cycle completion pulse advances result handoff; if suppressed the pipeline stalls awaiting completion, while spurious pulses retire incomplete data—both conditions impede forward progress.

Assets.Functionality: Single-cycle output-valid signal asserted when processing is done; indicates to the integrator that res_o contains a valid result for the instruction.
Assets.Justification: valid_o informs the system when res_o is ready; missing assertions cause consumers to wait indefinitely, while spurious assertions deliver invalid data, each reducing effective service availability.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the FPU rounding mode (frm) used by functional units and normalizer to select rounding behavior for operations.
Assets.Justification: csr_frm determines rounding behavior globally for FPU operations; corrupting this register changes numerical rounding semantics (and thus results) across operations. Incorrect or malicious changes to frm can silently alter computation outcomes, making its integrity important to the integrator.

Assets.Functionality: Stores accumulated floating-point exception flags (NX, UF, OF, DZ, NV) exposed to software via CSR reads/writes and auto-accumulation from fflags.
Assets.Justification: csr_fflags conveys exception conditions from FPU operations to software; if these flags are modified or suppressed the software view of FP exceptional behavior will be incorrect, possibly hiding faults or causing improper fault handling. Maintaining integrity of exception flags is necessary for correct system behavior and diagnostics.

Assets.Functionality: Input control that gates writes into FPU CSRs (frm and fflags) when asserted during CSR write operations.
Assets.Justification: csr_we_i authorizes updates to frm/fflags; spurious assertion overwrites rounding mode or flags, while suppression blocks legitimate writes—both yield incorrect arithmetic semantics and misleading status.

Assets.Functionality: Done signal from the normalizer/rounding unit indicating normalization & rounding (or i2f conversion) is finished and result/flags are valid.
Assets.Justification: The normalizer produces the definitive FP result for most arithmetic operations; if normalizer.done never asserts the core cannot finalize results, causing a DoS of FP functionality at integration level.

Assets.Functionality: Input data bus used to write values into the selected FPU CSR (fflags or frm) on a CSR write.
Assets.Justification: csr_wdata_i is the value committed to frm/fflags; corruption stores a wrong rounding mode or fabricates/erases exception flags, leading to incorrect computations and diagnostics.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit input selecting which FPU CSR (fflags, frm, fcsr) is accessed for read or write operations.
Assets.Justification: csr_addr_i determines which CSR is targeted; mis-selection causes writes/reads to hit the wrong register (e.g., fflags vs frm), corrupting control state and masking real error conditions.

Assets.Functionality: Two-bit comparator status from main ALU used by the FPU comparator logic to determine equal/less conditions for FEQ/FLT/FLE operations.
Assets.Justification: cmp_i encodes the ALU’s equality/ordering outcome; if corrupted or spoofed, FEQ/FLT/FLE yield wrong results and flags, misleading software and violating ISA semantics, so its integrity must be preserved.

Assets.Functionality: Latched operation class/funct encoding indicating which FPU operation (add/sub, mul, min/max, convert, compare, etc.) to execute.
Assets.Justification: funct_ff selects the FPU operation and controls downstream units; if altered, the engine executes the wrong function (e.g., add vs mul or min vs max), yielding incorrect results and flags.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit output bus carrying the FPU operation result (classifier, comparator, convert or normalized arithmetic result) back to the CPU pipeline.
Assets.Justification: res_o is the primary data interface by which the CPU receives FPU results; if res_o is suppressed, stuck, or otherwise made unavailable or incorrect at the integration boundary, the CPU cannot obtain correct results and system operation is impacted. At integration level, preventing valid result delivery is a denial-of-service on the CPU's use of the FPU.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit output asserted when FPU result on res_o is valid and ready to be consumed by the CPU pipeline.
Assets.Justification: valid_o gates acceptance of res_o by the CPU; if valid_o is withheld or spurious, the CPU may not capture a completed result or may accept invalid data, causing operation stalls or denial-of-service. Therefore the availability and correct assertion of valid_o is critical to system progress.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit input operand used as multiplicand or dividend; its sign bit is inspected for signed operations and it is used/negated internally for signed math.
Assets.Justification: If an attacker or faulty integrator can modify rs1_i, the arithmetic result (mul/div/rem) becomes incorrect and downstream software/state is corrupted. Protecting the integrity of the operand is therefore required to ensure correct computation.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit input operand used as multiplier or divisor; its sign is inspected/used to compute absolute values and to determine sign compensation.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or unauthorized modification of rs2_i directly changes multiplication/division behavior (wrong product, wrong quotient or remainder) and thus compromises correctness; integrity protection is needed for accurate results.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit result output that presents the final operation result (lower/upper product bits or div/rem result) when the unit indicates completion.
Assets.Justification: If res_o is corrupted (wrong bits driven) the consumer of the unit will receive incorrect computation results; preserving the integrity of the reported result is necessary to avoid incorrect program behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Current remainder register of the iterative restoring division algorithm; updated each cycle based on subtraction/restore decisions.
Assets.Justification: Manipulation of the remainder register corrupts the iterative division state and results in incorrect final remainder/quotient values. The integrity of this internal state is essential for correct division arithmetic.

Assets.Functionality: Working dividend/quotient shift register used during restoring division; accumulates quotient bits during iterations.
Assets.Justification: If div.quotient is corrupted, accumulated quotient bits will be wrong and final division results incorrect. Ensuring integrity of the quotient register is necessary to prevent result corruption.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag indicating whether rs1 should be treated as signed for the current operation; used for sign handling, abs/negation and final result compensation.
Assets.Justification: If this flag is incorrect the unit will apply wrong sign handling (wrong absolute values or incorrect sign compensation) and produce incorrect arithmetic results; integrity of this control bit is required to preserve correct computations.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag indicating whether rs2 should be treated as signed for the current operation; affects divisor/multiplier sign handling and product sign-extension decisions.
Assets.Justification: An incorrect rs2_is_signed causes wrong sign interpretation (e.g., incorrect abs(rs2) or p_sext behaviour) and leads to wrong product/quotient; protecting its integrity prevents incorrect arithmetic.

Assets.Functionality: Accumulator/product register holding the full (2*XLEN)-bit product during iterative multiply or the final product from the DSP path; source for res_o selection.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of mul.prod directly changes the arithmetic result (upper/lower halves used by different MUL operations), so its integrity is required to ensure correct outputs.

Assets.Functionality: Final division/rem result after sign compensation; selected as res_o for div/rem variants when operation completes.
Assets.Justification: If div.res is modified or computed incorrectly (including wrong sign compensation), the delivered quotient/remainder is incorrect and system behavior is compromised; integrity protection for the final result is therefore required.

Assets.Functionality: Single-cycle valid flag asserted when the co-processor has finished an operation and res_o contains the valid result (driven in S_DONE).
Assets.Justification: If valid_o is withheld or stuck low/high an integrator or CPU may be unable to detect completed operations (causing hangs or lost results), so availability of this signal is critical to prevent a denial-of-service of the execution flow.

Assets.Functionality: Iteration counter used by the serial multiplier/divider to count processing steps and determine when the operation completes.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with or faults in ctrl.cnt can prevent the operation from completing (infinite busy) or prematurely terminate it; maintaining correct counter behavior is necessary to ensure the unit can complete its work (avoid DoS or incorrect termination).

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle enable asserted when the unit finished processing to allow the result to be presented (used by operation_result to gate res_o).
Assets.Justification: If ctrl.out_en is suppressed or stuck, the result will not be presented on res_o even though computation finished, effectively denying the service for that instruction; availability of this enable is necessary to deliver results.

Assets.Functionality: Start handshake asserted when a multiplication instruction is decoded to initialize multiplier state and input registers for a new multiply.
Assets.Justification: Preventing or corrupting mul.start will stop new multiplication operations from being initiated (DoS of multiply capability); availability of the start handshake is required for correct operation sequencing.

Assets.Functionality: Start handshake asserted when a division instruction is decoded to initialize divider state and begin iterative division.
Assets.Justification: If div.start is blocked or malformed the divider will not begin operations, resulting in inability to perform division/remainder instructions; availability of this handshake is essential to avoid DoS of divide functionality.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit source operand fed into the serial shifter or the barrel shifter input layer; also provides the sign bit for arithmetic right shifts.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or tampering of rs1_i directly changes the shifted result (res_o) produced by the unit. The RTL shows rs1_i is loaded into shifter.sreg for serial operation and used as the input layer for the barrel shifter, so its integrity is essential to ensure correct computation.

Assets.Functionality: Index-sized vector that specifies the number of bit positions to shift; drives the serial shifter iteration count and the select lines of the barrel shifter stages.
Assets.Justification: Altering shamt_i changes how many positions the operand is shifted, directly impacting the result; the RTL assigns shamt_i to shifter.cnt for serial operation and indexes barrel-shifter muxes, so integrity of shamt_i is required to prevent incorrect or maliciously altered shift behavior.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit output that presents the operation result (after completion in the serial shifter or from the barrel shifter pipeline).
Assets.Justification: If res_o is blocked, stuck, or suppressed at integration, downstream logic cannot retrieve the computed shift result rendering the operation unusable; because res_o is the primary exported product of the unit as shown in the RTL, ensuring it is available is essential to avoid Denial-of-Service.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit shift register that holds the intermediate and final value during iterative (serial) shifting operations.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of shifter.sreg during the multi-cycle serial shift directly changes the final result; the RTL shows sreg being loaded from rs1_i and shifted each cycle, so its integrity is necessary to guarantee correct per-cycle state progression and final output.

Assets.Functionality: Index-sized counter storing the remaining shift iterations for the serial shifter; controls run/done behavior.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with shifter.cnt can change operation length (shorten/extend) or break completion detection, producing incorrect results or premature/late completion; because it directly controls the run/done semantics in the RTL, its integrity is required to preserve correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit internal signal that indicates whether arithmetic sign-extension must be applied during right shifts (depends on rs1_i MSB, funct12 and valid_cmd).
Assets.Justification: bs_sign selects arithmetic vs. logical right-shift behavior; if flipped or glitched, SRA can behave as SRL (or vice versa), breaking sign propagation and yielding incorrect arithmetic results, bounds checks, and address calculations—violating ISA correctness.

Assets.Functionality: Output flag indicating when res_o is valid: completion signal for the serial shifter and direct valid_cmd reflection for the barrel shifter.
Assets.Justification: If valid_o is suppressed or stuck false, consumers will not accept or act upon the produced result even if res_o holds data; conversely, if it is stuck true when no valid result exists, protocol-level errors can occur. The RTL explicitly uses valid_o to signal readiness, so its availability and correct toggling are required for normal operation.

Assets.Functionality: Registered version of the done condition used to present res_o at the correct cycle for the serial shifter.
Assets.Justification: shifter.done_ff aligns completion and result handoff; if suppressed or stuck low, the result is never presented and the controller waits indefinitely, stalling progress, while premature or stuck-high assertions expose stale/partial data and trigger false completions—both degrading availability.

Assets.Functionality: 16-bit compressed instruction input that supplies the decoder with opcode, funct3 and bit fields used to compute immediates, select decoding case branches, and determine reserved/illegal encodings.
Assets.Justification: Modification of instr_i changes the decoded 32-bit instruction semantics (immediates, registers, opcode/funct fields) and therefore directly corrupts program flow and behavior. Because the decompressor's purpose is to convert this exact input into a valid RV32 instruction, protecting correctness (integrity) of instr_i is dominant.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit decompressed instruction presented to downstream pipeline/stages; it mirrors the assembled 'decoded' value but forces OPCODE[1] to zero when an illegal encoding is detected.
Assets.Justification: If instr_o is blocked, forced to an invalid value, or withheld, the downstream CPU pipeline cannot receive valid instructions and execution can be halted (denial-of-service). While corruption is also harmful, the dominant impact of making the output unavailable is to prevent normal operation of the processor.

Assets.Functionality: Process variable that collects and sign-extends compressed-instruction bitfields to form 20-bit immediate values used to assemble jump/jal-type decoded immediates.
Assets.Justification: imm20_v is used to populate immediate fields of certain decompressed instructions (e.g., jumps); corruption of this value will change target addresses and control flow. Ensuring integrity of these assembled immediates is necessary to prevent unintended jumps or control-flow redirection.

Assets.Functionality: Process variable that collects and sign-extends compressed-instruction bitfields to form 12-bit immediates (branch-type or other small immediates) used when building the decoded instruction.
Assets.Justification: imm12_v contributes immediate bits to branch and other decompressed instructions; if these bits are corrupted the resulting instruction semantics (e.g., branch offsets or ALU immediates) will be wrong, potentially breaking program logic. Protecting imm12_v integrity prevents immediate-manipulation attacks that affect program correctness.

Assets.Functionality: Internal 32-bit vector that the decompressor process assembles from instr_i (fields, immediates, funct/opcode) and which is then propagated to instr_o (subject to 'illegal' modification).
Assets.Justification: Tampering with 'decoded' causes an incorrect instruction to be presented on instr_o, leading to corrupted execution and incorrect control/data behavior. Because 'decoded' is the immediate source for the output instruction, maintaining its correctness is critical to prevent instruction corruption.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the current fetch address (XLEN-bit) used to form word-aligned instruction bus requests and is advanced/realigned on each successful fetch or restart.
Assets.Justification: fetch.pc directly determines which instruction words are requested from memory; unauthorized modification or corruption can cause execution of wrong code or skipping of code regions. Protecting its integrity is essential because address corruption can subvert program control flow and lead to incorrect or malicious behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered restart/branch request flag used to synchronize clearing of the prefetch buffer (IPB) and to reinitialize the fetch engine after control transfers or resets.
Assets.Justification: If fetch.restart is modified while fetching, the prefetch FIFO can be cleared or erroneously kept cleared, leading to incorrect instruction sequencing. Maintaining the integrity of this control flag is required to ensure correct instruction stream reinitialization on branches or restarts.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered record of the privilege level associated with outstanding instruction fetches; forwarded to ibus_req_o.priv and updated during restarts from ctrl_i.cpu_priv.
Assets.Justification: If this privilege level is altered, instruction fetches may occur with incorrect rights, leading to privilege escalation or unintended access restrictions. Preserving its integrity ensures correct enforcement of privilege separation during instruction fetches.

Assets.Functionality: Availability indicators that signal whether valid data is present in each FIFO port and can be used by the issue engine to form/validate issued instructions.
Assets.Justification: ipb.avail gates the issuance of valid instructions; if an attacker can make avail indicate no data, the backend will be starved and instruction issue will halt. Protecting these indicators is necessary to prevent denial-of-service on instruction issue.

Assets.Functionality: Global CSR write enable input that, when asserted together with the ICC data CSR address, causes csr_wdata_i to be written into the TX FIFO (tx_fifo_we).
Assets.Justification: csr_we_i directly enables enqueuing of outgoing messages into the TX FIFO. If an integrator-deemed sensitive control (e.g., messages or command payloads) can be written via CSR writes, unauthorized or corrupted assertions of this signal could inject or corrupt transmitted data, so its dominant security concern is integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Global CSR read-enable input used (together with csr_addr_i) to generate the icc_tx_o.ack output when the data CSR is read; this ack plays a role in the link handshake/read behavior for transmitted data.
Assets.Justification: csr_re_i controls whether the TX FIFO is acknowledged/read and therefore whether queued outgoing messages are consumed. If this signal is suppressed or held inappropriately at integration level, the FIFO cannot be popped and the module can be forced into a denial-of-service condition (TX stalls/overflow), making availability the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Internal write-enable signal to the outgoing TX FIFO; asserted when a CSR data write occurs (csr_we_i with proper CSR address) and causes csr_wdata_i to be enqueued into the FIFO.
Assets.Justification: tx_fifo_we authorizes enqueue into the transmit FIFO; spurious assertion (especially when tx_fifo_free='0') injects duplicates/garbage or overwrites entries, while suppression drops legitimate writes—both corrupting the transmitted byte stream and violating data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Internal status signal driven by the TX FIFO that indicates whether free space is available; exposed via the ICC control CSR read (csr_rdata_o bit) so the integrator can observe whether a write will succeed.
Assets.Justification: tx_fifo_free reflects whether the outgoing queue can accept new messages and is used by integration logic to avoid overflows. Incorrect or manipulated status (stale/forced) can lead to prevented writes or incorrect operation of higher-level flow-control, causing message loss or denial-of-service, therefore its dominant impact is on availability.

Assets.Functionality: Provides the memory access address that is captured into the MAR and used to compute alignment and byte-enable signals for bus requests.
Assets.Justification: addr_i drives which memory location is accessed (it is captured into MAR and selects byte enables). If an integrator-level adversary can modify or inject wrong addr_i values the LSU will perform reads/writes to incorrect addresses, corrupting data or control flow; preserving the correctness of this input is therefore an integrity requirement.

Assets.Functionality: Supplies write data for store operations and AMOs; data is aligned/replicated into the bus request payload (dbus_req_o.data) depending on access size.
Assets.Justification: wdata_i is the payload written to memory; corruption or unauthorized modification of this input changes stored data and can corrupt program state or data structures. Ensuring the authenticity and correctness of wdata_i is therefore an integrity concern.

Assets.Functionality: Internal register that latches addr_i on request, used as the bus address source, for alignment decisions, and driven out as mar_o.
Assets.Justification: mar is the authoritative address used for accesses and for mar_o; corruption of mar will cause incorrect memory reads/writes and wrong fault address reporting. Maintaining mar correctness is therefore an integrity requirement.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flag computed from addr_i and funct3 to indicate whether the requested access is misaligned; it gates dbus_req_o.stb and contributes to err_o misalignment bits.
Assets.Justification: misaligned gates whether the LSU will assert the bus strobe (dbus_req_o.stb) and causes alignment error reporting; manipulation that forces misaligned to true can prevent issuance of memory requests and thus produce denial-of-service. Its dominant impact is availability of accesses.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered indicator combining dbus_rsp_i.err and pmp_fault_i used to present load/store bus errors through err_o and to influence arbiter state behaviour.
Assets.Justification: arbiter_err determines whether bus errors are reported to the control unit; if this flag is suppressed or spuriously set, error handling and trap flows will be incorrect. Accurate representation of bus/PMP errors is therefore an integrity property.

Assets.Functionality: Internal encoding of the requested atomic memory operation (derived from ir_funct12) that is forwarded to the data bus as dbus_req_o.amoop.
Assets.Justification: amo_cmd determines the semantics of atomic memory operations issued to the bus; corruption of this encoding can change operation semantics (e.g., turning SC into ADD) and thereby corrupt shared memory state. Preserving the correctness of amo_cmd is therefore an integrity requirement.

Assets.Functionality: Signals the CPU that the LSU is waiting for a data-bus response by presenting the inverse of dbus_rsp_i.ack.
Assets.Justification: wait_o controls CPU progress by indicating when the CPU must stall for a memory response; an attacker that can force this signal to stale/true (or prevent proper de-assertion) can cause denial-of-service or lock up downstream logic. Therefore its availability and correct toggling are availability-critical.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates a memory protection (PMP) violation; it is considered when buffering arbiter errors and gating/stalling bus requests (also contributes to arbiter_err).
Assets.Justification: When asserted pmp_fault_i prevents the LSU from issuing a bus strobe and contributes to arbiter_err; an adversary able to assert or hold this line can repeatedly block accesses and cause denial-of-service. The primary impact is availability of memory operations.

Assets.Functionality: Tracks whether a memory access request is pending; it is set from lsu_req and cleared on dbus_rsp_i.ack or cpu_trap, and it gates rdata_o/err_o logic.
Assets.Justification: If arbiter_req becomes stuck or is falsely asserted/cleared the LSU can be prevented from issuing new requests or will miss/duplicate responses, causing stalls or deadlock. Therefore ensuring correct request progress is an availability concern.

Assets.Functionality: Per-region 8-bit configuration registers that hold R/W/X permissions, mode bits (TOR/NA4/NAPOT/OFF) and the lock bit; used to determine how each PMP region behaves and whether writes to region CSRs are allowed.
Assets.Justification: pmpcfg defines region permissions, matching mode, and the lock state; if corrupted, it can silently grant or revoke execute/read/write access or clear the lock, enabling bypass or disabling of PMP protections and yielding incorrect access decisions.

Assets.Functionality: Per-region address CSRs used as bounds/encoded addresses for TOR/NA4/NAPOT region matching; these values feed the comparator logic to decide whether an access hits a region.
Assets.Justification: pmpaddr encodes region boundaries for TOR/NA4/NAPOT; any bit flip or miswrite shifts or enlarges/shrinks regions so hits/misses are computed incorrectly, enabling unauthorized accesses or overblocking legitimate ones.

Assets.Functionality: Provides CSR read-back data for PMP configuration and address CSRs (pmpcfg/pmpaddr) to the CPU CSR read interface; packed from internal cfg_rd32/addr_rd to present current PMP permissions and region boundaries.
Assets.Justification: csr_o is the software-visible truth for PMP state; if corrupted, software observes incorrect permissions/locks or region bounds and may make unsafe decisions or fail to detect tampering, undermining enforcement of memory protection.

Assets.Functionality: Supply of the load/store address used by the PMP when time-multiplexing between instruction fetch and data accesses; selected into acc_addr for permission comparison against pmpaddr/pmpcfg to determine match and allow signals.
Assets.Justification: addr_ls_i is the address the PMP evaluates; if altered, comparisons are made against the wrong location, allowing unauthorized accesses or incorrectly blocking legitimate ones.

Assets.Functionality: Vector of per-region signals that indicate whether the current acc_addr falls into the corresponding region according to the configured mode (TOR/NA4/NAPOT/OFF).
Assets.Justification: match drives region selection for allow/fail decisions; corruption yields false hits or misses (e.g., due to wrong mask/compare), misapplying permissions and enabling protection bypass or unintended denial.

Assets.Functionality: Vector of per-region computed permission bits (R/W/X) that indicate whether a given access type is permitted for that region, taking into account privilege level and lock semantics.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of allow bits directly causes incorrect permit/deny decisions for memory accesses (either enabling unauthorized access or denying legitimate operations). Maintaining the integrity of allow is required for correct enforcement of PMP policies.

Assets.Functionality: Output signal that indicates a PMP permission violation (permission fault) after prioritized region checks and allow/fail logic; asserted to signal access error to the CPU (ignored in debug mode).
Assets.Justification: The correctness of this signal is critical to the system's enforcement and reporting of access violations: if an attacker can tamper with or suppress fault_o, real permission violations can be hidden; if forced asserted, benign accesses can be incorrectly flagged. Thus protecting the integrity of this indicator is essential to maintain correct security behavior.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit destination operand input that is written into the selected register entry when a write is enabled by the register-file control logic.
Assets.Justification: rd_i is the source of new register contents; if an attacker can modify or control rd_i the register file will be written with incorrect values and CPU state will be corrupted. Protecting rd_i integrity is therefore critical to prevent unintended or malicious data corruption.

Assets.Functionality: Array of register entries (2**addr_bits_c entries of XLEN bits) that holds all CPU register values (including general-purpose registers and x0). It is read by rs1/rs2/rs3 ports and written by the write path.
Assets.Justification: reg_file holds the processor architectural state: corrupting entries changes program behavior and dataflow across the CPU. Ensuring the integrity of this storage is dominant because erroneous or malicious modifications directly break correctness and can subvert the system.

Assets.Functionality: Multiplexed 5-bit address signal selecting either rd (write destination), forced-zero address, or rs1 (read source) depending on control conditions; used to index the reg_file for the single multiplexed port in the FPGA-style implementation.
Assets.Justification: opa_addr determines which register is read or written on the shared port; corrupting opa_addr will cause reads/writes to target wrong registers, producing incorrect operand values or overwriting the wrong destination. Therefore integrity of this address selection is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Internal boolean signal indicating that the selected destination register address equals zero (x0). It is used to suppress normal writes to x0 (which should remain zero) unless explicitly forced via rf_zero_we.
Assets.Justification: rd_zero controls protection of the architectural zero register; if rd_zero is manipulated an attacker could enable writes to x0 or block intended protection, changing guaranteed semantics and corrupting software assumptions. Protecting rd_zero integrity preserves correctness of register semantics.

Assets.Functionality: Internal write-enable signal that gates writes into the register file (derived from control bus signals and rd_zero). When low, writes are suppressed; when high, rd_i is committed to the addressed register.
Assets.Justification: rf_we determines whether rd_i is committed to the register file; if rf_we is tampered with an adversary can suppress legitimate writes or induce unauthorized writes, leading to corrupted register state and incorrect operation. Thus integrity of rf_we is essential.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit output presenting the value read from the register addressed by rf_rs1 (or by the multiplexed opa_addr in the FPGA-style implementation) each clock cycle for use by the core's execution units.
Assets.Justification: rs1_o is required by downstream pipeline stages to fetch operand data; if rs1_o is blocked, stuck, or withheld at integration level it causes the CPU to stall or malfunction (denial-of-service). Ensuring availability of rs1_o is therefore critical for correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit output presenting the value read from the register addressed by rf_rs2 each clock cycle for use by the core's execution units.
Assets.Justification: rs2_o supplies another essential operand for instruction execution; if its output is blocked or driven incorrectly at integration, instruction execution can be prevented or severely disrupted, constituting a denial-of-service to normal operation.

Assets.Functionality: XLEN-bit optional third source operand output (enabled when RS3_EN) that presents the value read from the rs3 address (derived from ir_funct12[11:7]) for certain instructions; tied to zero when disabled.
Assets.Justification: When RS3_EN is used, rs3_o is required by consumers expecting a third operand; if this output is made unavailable or tampered with at integration level it can prevent correct instruction execution or tests, causing denial-of-service of functionality that depends on rs3.

Assets.Functionality: Input that enables the authenticator. When low the module clears the authentication state and disables setting authentication; when high writes (we_i + wdata_i) may set authentication.
Assets.Justification: Toggling this input to '0' clears authentication and effectively prevents the debugger from being unlocked until re-enabled, enabling a denial-of-service at integration level. An attacker controlling or spoofing this signal can repeatedly clear or hold the module disabled, blocking normal debug access.

Assets.Functionality: Write strobe sampled on clock edges; when high the module samples wdata_i(0) and may update the internal authenticated state.
Assets.Justification: This control directly gates modification of the authentication state: an attacker able to assert or suppress we_i can maliciously set or prevent updates to authentication, corrupting the intended authentication flow. Therefore it is an integrity-critical control because it can change sensitive state (authenticated_q).

Assets.Functionality: Output that reflects the internal authenticated state and is used by the debugger to determine whether access/unlock is granted.
Assets.Justification: This output is the effective unlock signal for the on-chip debugger; if it can be manipulated (forged high or forced low) the attacker can improperly grant or deny access. Protecting its integrity is critical because unauthorized modification directly impacts control decisions outside the module.

Assets.Functionality: Internal flip-flop holding the authentication state; set by sampled wdata_i(0) when we_i='1' and cleared by reset or when enable_i='0'; drives valid_o.
Assets.Justification: This internal register is the canonical sensitive state that gates debugger unlock; altering it (via legitimate or malicious means) changes whether the debugger is considered authenticated. Because modification of this element directly affects access control, its integrity is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Per-hart vector output used to request one or multiple harts to enter debug/halt state; asserted when the DM requests halt for the selected hart(s) and gated by dmactive and authentication.
Assets.Justification: If halt_req_o is unavailable or suppressed, the debug module cannot stop a hart for inspection or safe program-buffer execution, preventing debugger-driven control flows and effectively denying debug functionality. Blocking this output could therefore be used as a denial-of-service against debug operations and coordinated debug sequences.

Assets.Functionality: Active-low SoC reset output asserted when the DM requests a non-debug-module reset (ndmreset) while DM is active and authentication (if present) allows it.
Assets.Justification: ndmrstn_o is used to request a full SoC reset; if this signal is blocked or spuriously held inactive the DM cannot perform expected reset operations or could force resets unexpectedly. Either denial (preventing reset) or unintended assertion (forcing resets) impacts system availability and correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: Memory-mapped data exchange register used for transferring data between the DM and the CPU (DM.data0). It is the source/destination for GPR<->DM transfers controlled by abstract commands and program-buffer sequences.
Assets.Justification: dci.data_reg can contain arbitrary CPU register or memory values moved via abstract commands, including sensitive material (e.g., keys or credentials) originating from a hart. Unauthorized reads or external observation of this register leaks potentially confidential data, so it represents a confidentiality risk.

Assets.Functionality: Flag from the optional authenticator indicating successful authentication; when set, authenticated read/write enables (dmi_*_auth) are permitted.
Assets.Justification: If auth.valid is spoofed or improperly cleared/set, it changes whether protected DM registers are writable/readable, directly affecting who can change DM configuration or read data. Maintaining the integrity of this flag is critical to prevent unauthorized writes/reads and preserve access-control semantics.

Assets.Functionality: Drives the serial data output on the JTAG TDO pin (updated on TCK falling edge) and presents the LSB of the currently active register (IR or selected DR) or the bypass bit to the external JTAG chain.
Assets.Justification: TDO is the outward-facing serial channel that exposes the contents of internal registers (IDCODE, DTMCS, DMI) to an external observer. Any sensitive read data contained in the DMI register or rdata will be shifted out on TDO, so control or observation of this signal can leak confidential information.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the 32-bit read data returned from the debug module interface (captured from dmi_rsp_i) and is presented back to the TAP via tap_reg.dmi_nxt on capture.
Assets.Justification: This register is the canonical storage for data read from the debug target; its contents are propagated into the TAP-readable DMI register and therefore can be exposed externally. If the debug target contains secrets, the rdata value is a direct confidentiality risk.

Assets.Functionality: Provides the serial data input for shifting bits into the instruction register (IREG) or the currently selected data register (DR) during IR_SHIFT/DR_SHIFT phases; used to load instructions, DTMCS and DMI payloads (address, wdata, op).
Assets.Justification: An attacker who controls or tampers with TDI can inject bits that change the instruction register, DTMCS or the DMI register contents, causing unauthorized writes or configuration changes. By corrupting shifted-in data, TDI can modify control/state and thus corrupt sensitive operations and the data-path.

Assets.Functionality: Controls the TAP controller state machine transitions (on TCK rising edges) and thereby determines when IR/DR capture, shift, update or bypass operations occur.
Assets.Justification: TMS selects TAP states that permit capture/update of registers (including DTMCS and DMI). An attacker that manipulates TMS can force unexpected state transitions that enable illicit updates to internal registers or replay/skip update events, leading to corrupted control and register contents.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the 7-bit DMI target address extracted from the DMI shift register during update and used to address subsequent DMI transactions.
Assets.Justification: If the address is modified or corrupted, read/write operations will target unintended locations, possibly corrupting sensitive registers or memory. Ensuring the correctness of the address field is necessary to prevent unintended or malicious operations on the debug target.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates that a DMI transaction is in progress and prevents acceptance of new DMI requests until the current transaction completes (cleared when dmi_rsp_i.ack is set).
Assets.Justification: If busy is stuck asserted (or forced), new DMI accesses are blocked and the TAP cannot issue further requests, causing a denial-of-service on debug access. Availability of the debug interface depends on correct busy behavior.

Assets.Functionality: External serial clock input that is sampled and synchronized to produce tck_rising/tck_falling events which drive TAP FSM transitions and shift/update timing for IR/DR operations.
Assets.Justification: The TCK signal is required for any JTAG shifting or state transitions; if TCK is absent, stuck, or manipulated, the TAP cannot perform shifts/updates and the DTM cannot be driven, resulting in denial of debug functionality.

Assets.Functionality: Four separate byte-level arrays holding the DMEM content (bits 7–0, 15–8, 23–16, 31–24). Selective writes occur via bus_req_i.ben, while read operations combine the four slices into a 32-bit word.
Assets.Justification: These arrays are the canonical storage for program and data values: unauthorized modification (incorrect writes, corruption) will directly alter stored state and cause incorrect program behavior. Protecting the correctness of their contents is therefore primarily an integrity concern.

Assets.Functionality: Derived directly from bus_req_i.addr(addr_hi_c downto 2), this unsigned index selects the addressed word for reads and writes.
Assets.Justification: addr determines which memory word is read or written; tampering or corruption of this signal will redirect accesses to wrong locations and thereby corrupt data or control flow, so its integrity is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Collects outputs from the four byte slices to form the 32-bit word returned on bus_rsp_o.data.
Assets.Justification: rdata conveys the value returned from memory to the bus; if rdata is corrupted (wrong byte assembly or stuck values) the requester receives incorrect data, so protecting the correctness of rdata is an integrity requirement.

Assets.Functionality: A registered signal that indicates when a valid read request is present. It controls presentation of rdata onto bus_rsp_o.data.
