Assets.Justification: rden controls whether read data is actually presented on the response bus; if rden is suppressed, stuck low, or otherwise manipulated, valid read responses will be withheld causing a denial-of-service of memory reads, making availability the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Byte-wide memory arrays that together implement the 32-bit instruction memory when IMEM is configured as RAM; they store the four bytes of each instruction word and are written under byte-enable during bus write accesses and read to form rdata.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the memory arrays directly modifies the stored instructions; corrupted or maliciously changed bytes will cause incorrect instructions to be fetched and executed. Because these arrays determine the code executed by the processor, their integrity is critical to correct and secure operation.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit register/vector holding the word read from the instruction memory (ROM or RAM); updated on clock edges and presented on the bus response data output when a read is active.
Assets.Justification: If rdata is corrupted or altered between memory read and presentation, the processor will receive incorrect instruction words leading to wrong execution. Maintaining the integrity of rdata is necessary to ensure the fetched instruction matches the stored memory contents.

Assets.Functionality: Unsigned, word-aligned address derived from the incoming bus request address (addr_hi_c downto 2); used to index the memory arrays for read and write accesses.
Assets.Justification: If the address used to access memory is corrupted or manipulated, the module will return or overwrite the wrong instruction words, altering program flow. The addr signal directly controls which memory locations are read or written, so its integrity is essential to prevent instruction substitution or control-flow attacks.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit registered read-enable that indicates an active read request (bus_req_i.stb and not bus_req_i.rw); it controls whether rdata is presented on bus_rsp_o.data (rdata when rden='1', otherwise zeros).
Assets.Justification: If rden is suppressed or stuck low, valid read data will be gated off and the bus response will present zeros, effectively denying instruction fetches and causing a denial-of-service of processor execution. Thus the dominant concern for rden is availability of instruction data to the bus master.

Assets.Functionality: A 32 bit access address the cache memory uses to derive tag, index, and word offset for tag or status checks and for addressing the data array.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the address will redirect reads/writes to wrong tag/index/offset locations, causing incorrect data to be stored or returned and breaking memory coherence. Because addr_i controls which block and word are accessed, its corruption directly results in logical data corruption and incorrect tag updates.

Assets.Functionality: Input that clears the valid flag of the currently addressed cache block for flush or error handling.
Assets.Justification: Improper assertion or suppression of inval_i can lead to use of stale or invalid data (if inval suppressed) or unnecessary loss of valid data (if asserted erroneously). Because invalidation changes the valid bit for an indexed block, corrupting this control disrupts correct memory behavior and data correctness.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered flag that latches an incoming host request across state machine cycles so pending accesses can be serviced.
Assets.Justification: If this latch is prevented from being set or is stuck, pending host accesses will not be serviced and the cache controller will fail to progress, effectively causing a denial-of-service for the host. ctrl.buf_req is the controller's integration-level gate for servicing requests, so loss or corruption of this signal results in unavailability of normal memory access.

Assets.Functionality: Buffered flag that remembers a pending flush or synchronization request across FSM transitions.
Assets.Justification: If buf_sync cannot record or propagate a pending flush/fence, required flush operations may not be performed, which can block higher-level operations that wait for cache synchronization and thus produce denial-of-service or stalled system behavior. Because this signal schedules flush operations at integration level, its absence or being stuck prevents completion of required sync actions.

Assets.Functionality: Status input from the cache memory that indicates whether the current address is a hit. The controller uses it to choose between read or write paths and whether to replace or respond directly.
Assets.Justification: If sta_hit is manipulated (stuck or spoofed), the controller's control flow is disrupted: perpetual misses may trigger excessive downloads/uploads, and perpetual hits may prevent necessary downloads, both leading to functional breakdown or effective denial-of-service. As the primary decision bit for access progression, incorrect hit signals can prevent proper servicing of requests and stall operation.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level signal that indicates the cache is globally 'clean' (no dirty lines) synchronized with downstream memory; asserted by the control engine when the internal cache memory reports clean and the controller is idle.
Assets.Justification: System-level synchronization (fence semantics) depends on this signal to know when the cache is safe/clean; if this signal is suppressed or manipulated the integrator may stall or incorrectly assume completion, causing denial-of-service or broken synchronization. Therefore its availability/trustworthiness is critical for correct system progress.

Assets.Functionality: One-bit internal selector that chooses which host port (A when '0', B when '1') is currently driving the downstream device request bus and which host receives the device response.
Assets.Justification: The selector determines which master's address/data/control are forwarded and which master's response is returned. An attacker or fault that corrupts 'sel' can cause transactions to be routed incorrectly (wrong master served or responses delivered to the wrong origin), directly violating the integrity of bus transactions.

Assets.Functionality: Strobe signal generated by the arbiter FSM that enables/indicates the selected request is being forwarded to the downstream device (x_req_o.stb).
Assets.Justification: If 'stb' is suppressed or stuck low, valid requests from the selected host will not be forwarded, causing denial-of-service for that master. Conversely, spurious assertion could cause phantom transactions; both behaviors primarily impact availability of bus services.

Assets.Functionality: Sticky/internal flag that records and holds a pending request from host port A until it is served by the arbiter.
Assets.Justification: This signal preserves pending A requests across cycles; if manipulated it can either permanently block A from getting service (if cleared) or permanently indicate a pending request (if stuck), causing starvation or denial-of-service for other masters — an availability impact.

Assets.Functionality: Sticky/internal flag that records and holds a pending request from host port B until it is served by the arbiter.
Assets.Justification: Analogous to a_req: tampering with 'b_req' can cause B to be prevented from accessing the bus or to monopolize arbitration, resulting in denial-of-service or unfair starvation of other masters, impacting availability.

Assets.Functionality: One-hot 4-bit vector produced by the gateway address decoder that indicates which section port (A,B,C or X/void) a host request address maps to and gates the corresponding port's STB.
Assets.Justification: port_sel determines routing of every host address to a specific device region; an incorrect or corrupted selection will redirect reads/writes to the wrong device/region, causing data corruption, leakage between address spaces, or privilege violations — an integrity breach.

Assets.Functionality: Internal error flag asserted by the gateway's bus monitor when a monitored access errors out or times out; forwarded to the host response error output (rsp_o.err).
Assets.Justification: Because keeper.err is propagated as the host error signal, false assertion will cause the host to treat accesses as failed and may abort operations or trigger exceptions, producing denial-of-service or degraded operation — an availability concern.

Assets.Functionality: Internal qualifier used by the keeper logic to disable timeout enforcement for certain accesses (e.g., X-port/void redirections); influences whether the keeper generates a timeout error.
Assets.Justification: Manipulating keeper.halt can either hide hung/long transactions (preventing error detection) or incorrectly enable timeouts; both outcomes can allow stuck transactions or spuriously terminate operations, impacting availability of the bus subsystem.

Assets.Functionality: FSM state register of the AMO read-modify-write controller that sequences read, execute and write phases required to implement atomic memory operations.
Assets.Justification: The FSM enforces correct atomic sequencing; corruption of this state can break atomicity (e.g., skip read or write phases), causing race conditions, incorrect memory updates, or inconsistent return values — directly compromising memory operation integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit result from the AMO data ALU (swap/add/xor/and/or/min/max) which is used as the write-data during the atomic write phase.
Assets.Justification: alu_res becomes the data written back to memory for AMO operations; if altered, the stored value will be incorrect and memory integrity is violated. This directly affects the correctness of atomic operations and program behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Register that holds the write operand supplied by the core for use by the AMO ALU when computing the atomic write result.
Assets.Justification: arbiter.wdata is an input to the ALU and influences the resulting write value; unauthorized modification corrupts the computed ALU result and therefore the value written to memory, breaking data integrity for AMO operations.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit read-data input from the external bus. When a transaction is pending (pending(1) = '1') this signal is forwarded into bus_rsp.data and delivered to the host.
Assets.Justification: xbus_dat_i becomes the CPU-visible read value when pending(1) is set; if altered or spoofed, incorrect data is injected into architectural state and hides true bus behavior, violating end-to-end data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 2-bit internal state vector that tracks arbiter/transaction state (idle, single access, atomic load/store sequencing). It gates timeout counting, xbus_cyc_o behavior and the generation of bus_rsp.ack/err.
Assets.Justification: pending encodes handshake/atomic sequencing and qualifies ack/err; corruption misorders commits, breaks atomicity, or fabricates completions, yielding silent protocol misuse and incorrect bus_rsp results—hence its integrity is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Acknowledge input from the external bus used by the arbiter to complete/advance transactions; used to generate bus_rsp.ack when pending(1) is asserted.
Assets.Justification: xbus_ack_i completes the transfer handshake; if suppressed, requests never retire and the system stalls, while spurious assertions advance state without valid data, causing retries or lockups—reducing availability.

Assets.Functionality: Error input from the external bus that aborts pending transactions, causes the arbiter to clear pending state, and contributes to bus_rsp.err (also combined with timeout).
Assets.Justification: xbus_err_i terminates faulty transactions; if suppressed, the arbiter can wait indefinitely on bad targets, and if asserted spuriously, valid transactions are aborted—both harming forward progress and availability.

Assets.Functionality: Outputs the 32-bit transaction address onto the Wishbone-compatible external bus, derived from the internal request field (bus_req.addr).
Assets.Justification: xbus_adr_o selects the external destination/source; corruption misaddresses transfers, causing reads/writes to unintended locations and silent state corruption—therefore address integrity is essential.

Assets.Functionality: Transfers 32-bit write data from the CPU to the external bus, driven by bus_req.data.
Assets.Justification: xbus_dat_o is the value committed to external memory/peripherals; modifications in flight store incorrect data and violate end-to-end data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Internal signal that is asserted when the timeout counter reaches TIMEOUT_VAL; used to abort/flag stalled transactions and is combined into bus_rsp.err and arbiter decisions to clear pending state.
Assets.Justification: timeout bounds how long the bus may wait; if never asserted, the system can hang on unresponsive devices, while premature assertion aborts valid transfers—both degrade availability.

Assets.Functionality: Internal counter that increments while a transaction is pending and drives the timeout signal when it reaches the configured TIMEOUT_VAL.
Assets.Justification: timecnt determines when timeouts fire; incorrect counting delays or prevents aborts (hang) or triggers early timeouts (spurious aborts), impeding forward progress and system availability.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit external GPIO output vector driven from the internal port_out register and presented to the outside world (only lower GPIO_NUM bits used).
Assets.Justification: The correctness of gpio_o is essential for correct external-device control; unauthorized or accidental modification of these output values would change device behavior. Thus protecting the integrity of the output bits is the dominant security concern.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit external GPIO input vector sampled into internal registers (port_in/port_in2) and used for read-back and interrupt detection.
Assets.Justification: External input values influence internal state (irq_trig, irq_pend) and can change system control flow; a malicious or corrupted input can force incorrect behavior or false triggers. Therefore, ensuring the integrity (i.e., correctness and intended values) of gpio_i is the dominant concern at integration level.

Assets.Functionality: Internal register that holds values written by the bus and is driven onto gpio_o to produce the module's external outputs.
Assets.Justification: port_out determines the signals presented on gpio_o; tampering or corruption of this register directly alters outputs and can cause incorrect control of external devices. Protecting the integrity of port_out is therefore critical.

Assets.Functionality: Per-pin configuration bits that select trigger polarity (high/low for level, rising/falling for edge) and combine with irq_typ to form irq_trig conditions.
Assets.Justification: Altering irq_pol changes which input level or edge generates a trigger, which can cause incorrect interrupt behavior; maintaining the integrity of these polarity bits is necessary to preserve intended operation.

Assets.Functionality: Per-pin register that gates whether detected trigger events can set/hold pending interrupts in irq_pend (only enabled pins create pending interrupts).
Assets.Justification: Modifying irq_en enables or disables the generation of pending interrupts per pin; unauthorized changes can suppress or enable interrupts leading to incorrect system control. Integrity of irq_en is therefore the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Per-pin control signals written via the bus to clear pending interrupts (a '0' clears the corresponding irq_pend bit, '1' preserves it); used to acknowledge/clear interrupts.
Assets.Justification: Control of irq_clrn directly affects whether pending interrupts remain or are cleared; corruption or unauthorized writes can clear critical pending interrupts or prevent clearing, altering interrupt semantics. Thus integrity of irq_clrn is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit interrupt output asserted when any enabled GPIO pending interrupt exists (OR-reduction of irq_pend) to notify the CPU.
Assets.Justification: If cpu_irq_o is unavailable (stuck or suppressed), the CPU will not be informed of GPIO events, causing denial-of-service for interrupt-driven operation. The primary risk is loss of notification/availability rather than secrecy or modification of data.

Assets.Functionality: Combinational per-pin signals computed from port_in, port_in2, irq_typ and irq_pol that indicate when the configured interrupt condition has occurred.
Assets.Justification: If the trigger computation is corrupted (wrong irq_trig values), it will produce false or missing triggers and thus wrong irq_pend updates. This affects correctness of interrupt detection and is therefore an integrity concern.

Assets.Functionality: Synchronized capture of the external gpio_i inputs every clock; used for read-back and for generating interrupt trigger conditions.
Assets.Justification: If port_in sampling is unavailable or blocked, the module cannot observe external inputs nor generate correct interrupts, effectively denying normal input-driven operation. Availability of timely, sampled input values is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Drives the external clock-generator enable line from the timer global enable control bit; when asserted it allows the external clkgen to provide prescaled clock taps used by the timer.
Assets.Justification: If this enable output is forced inactive or blocked at integration, the external clock generator will not provide ticks to the timer and the timer will cease functioning (denial-of-service). The timer's ability to operate depends on this output being asserted when enabled, so its availability is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Signals the processor/host that the timer count reached the programmed threshold by reflecting the internal pending interrupt flag (irq_pnd).
Assets.Justification: If the IRQ line is suppressed, tied off, or otherwise unavailable at integration, the system will not be notified of timer events, preventing intended interrupt-driven behavior (denial-of-service). The primary role of this port is event delivery, so availability is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Holds the timer global enable bit and the three prescaler selection bits that select which bit of the clkgen vector is used as timer tick; written via bus writes to the control register.
Assets.Justification: Unauthorized or incorrect modification of the control bits (enable or prescaler selection) changes timer behavior — enabling/disabling the timer or selecting a different tick rate — which corrupts expected timing and operation. Because these are writable control fields that directly alter operation, their integrity is the dominant requirement.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit threshold/compare value written over the bus that the counter is compared against to produce timer.match and hence an interrupt when reached.
Assets.Justification: A malicious or erroneous write to the threshold changes when match events and interrupts occur, altering system timing and semantics. Since this register is externally writable and directly controls when timer events fire, preserving its correctness (integrity) is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Internal pending interrupt flag set when timer.match occurs while enabled and cleared by irq_clr (bus write); directly drives the irq_o output.
Assets.Justification: If irq_pnd is spuriously cleared or prevented from being set (for example via unauthorized clear requests or prevented propagation), timer events will not be delivered to the system, causing a denial-of-service for interrupt-driven functionality. The signal's availability to reflect actual match events is therefore essential.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit external vector of clock taps from the clock generator from which a single bit is selected (via prescaler bits) to produce timer.tick.
Assets.Justification: clkgen_i provides the time base for timer.tick; if taps are stalled, missing, or corrupted, the timer cannot advance (or advances at the wrong rate), breaking timeouts/periodic events and causing hangs or premature triggers that degrade system availability.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit vector holding the current state of each hardware spinlock; each bit is set on a claim (bus read to the selected lock) and cleared on a release (bus write) for the corresponding lock index.
Assets.Justification: The correctness of lock_q is critical to enforce mutual exclusion: if bits are corrupted or manipulated, resources may be incorrectly claimed or released, causing incorrect arbitration or privilege escalation between masters. Protecting the integrity of lock_q prevents unauthorized modification of lock ownership which would directly alter system behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Per-lock selection signals derived from bus_req_i.addr(6 downto 2) that indicate which of the 32 spinlocks is targeted by the current bus transaction. sel(i) gates updates to lock_q(i) and is used to mask the lock_q bits when returning an individual lock's state in the bus response.
Assets.Justification: sel controls which lock is read or written; tampering with or corrupting the selection logic can cause writes/reads to affect the wrong lock, leading to incorrect ownership or unauthorized access to critical sections. This directly undermines the integrity of lock operations and thus the integrity of protected resources.

Assets.Functionality: Asynchronous serial data line that drives the WS281x/NeoPixel LED chain; the serial TX engine toggles this line to emit data bits and to perform RESET (strobe) timing.
Assets.Justification: neoled_o carries the pixel bitstream and RESET pulses; any unauthorized modification or tampering of the signal (timing or level) directly corrupts displayed colors or commands. Because it is the primary data-bearing interface to the LEDs, protecting its integrity is essential.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level enable flag for the module; it is sampled into the serial FSM (MSB of serial.state), drives clkgen_en_o, and inversely controls tx_fifo.clear to flush the FIFO when disabled.
Assets.Justification: If ctrl.enable is deasserted (or corrupted) the TX engine is disabled and the FIFO cleared, preventing any LED updates and causing a denial-of-service of the NeoPixel output. Thus availability of the LED functionality depends on the correct value of this control.

Assets.Functionality: Output enable that activates an external clock/pulse generator when the module is enabled; the selected bit of the external clkgen_i vector is used as the internal pulse clock for precise WS281x timing.
Assets.Justification: If clkgen_en_o is not asserted (or the external clock generator is disabled), the internal pulse timing source may be missing or incorrect and the module cannot properly drive NeoPixels, effectively denying LED operation. Therefore the availability of correct timing depends on this signal.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit shift register that holds the current pixel data being transmitted (shifted MSB-first); serial.next_bit is selected from sreg depending on mode and is shifted each GETBIT cycle.
Assets.Justification: serial.sreg contains the actual bits that will be emitted; any corruption or unintended modification of the shift register contents corrupts the outgoing bitstream and thus LED output. Protecting its integrity is therefore essential to ensure correct transmission.

Assets.Functionality: Control register fields that define the pulse period (t_total)in pulse-clock ticks; the serial FSM uses these values to generate correct WS281x duty cycles and strobe durations.
Assets.Justification: t_total defines the overall bit period for the WS281x protocol; corruption skews the symbol timing window so that even correct high-times are interpreted wrongly, producing bit slips and corrupted LED data patterns.

Assets.Functionality: Control register fields that define the high-time for '0' and '1' bits (t0_high, t1_high) in pulse-clock ticks; the serial FSM uses these values to generate correct WS281x duty cycles and strobe durations.
Assets.Justification: t0_high/t1_high set the duty thresholds that encode logic ‘0’ vs ‘1’; if altered or swapped, the transmitter mis-encodes symbols and the LEDs decode the wrong bitstream, causing silent data corruption (wrong colors/patterns).

Assets.Functionality: 3-bit index selecting which bit of the external clkgen_i vector is sampled as the internal pulse clock (serial.pulse_clk) used to time pulse increments for transmission.
Assets.Justification: If clk_prsc is modified at runtime or set incorrectly, the selected pulse clock may be inappropriate and the resulting pulse timings will be incorrect, corrupting transmitted data. Protecting this selection prevents unintended timing shifts and data corruption.

Assets.Functionality: When asserted, a FIFO write enqueues a strobe/RESET command instead of normal pixel data; the serial FSM uses this bit-per-entry to enter the STROBE state and send a long RESET low period.
Assets.Justification: An unexpected or corrupted strobe bit will cause a FIFO entry to be treated as a RESET rather than pixel data (or vice versa), altering LED chain state and corrupting intended updates. Ensuring the strobe bit's integrity prevents unintended resets or lost pixel frames.

Assets.Functionality: Concatenation of ctrl.strobe, ctrl.mode and bus write data that is enqueued into the TX FIFO for later transmission by the serial engine.
Assets.Justification: tx_fifo.wdata is the source of all transmitted LED words; corruption of these bits (mode/strobe or payload) results in incorrect transmissions to the LED chain. Protecting the integrity of write data is required to ensure correct output.

Assets.Functionality: Physical 1-Wire bus input sampled and synchronized by the serial engine (serial.wire_in) to detect device presence and to read data bits from attached 1-Wire devices.
Assets.Justification: onewire_i is the authoritative source of all received bits and presence information. An attacker or misbehaving device that manipulates the physical line will directly change sampled values and presence detection, corrupting the data presented to the CPU and causing erroneous protocol behavior, so integrity is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Output that actively pulls the 1-Wire bus low (drive) or releases it (tristate) under control of the serial engine (serial.wire_lo / serial.wire_hi) to implement reset, write and timing slots.
Assets.Justification: If onewire_o cannot assert the required drive state (for example if the external integration holds the line forced-high/low or the pad is unavailable), the controller cannot generate proper time slots or reset pulses, preventing normal operation (denial-of-service). Availability is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Control register bit that gates the entire module: it is used by the serial engine (serial.state(2) <= ctrl.enable), drives clkgen_en_o and enables clearing/clocking behavior across the block.
Assets.Justification: ctrl.enable globally enables or disables the controller; an unexpected or malicious change to this bit prevents the controller from operating at all, causing a clear denial-of-service to any software relying on the peripheral.

Assets.Functionality: Write-only control bit used to clear/reset the TX and RX FIFOs (fifo.tx_clr and fifo.rx_clr) when asserted; the bit auto-clears in the bus-access logic.
Assets.Justification: Asserting ctrl.clear removes queued commands and received data, directly modifying or eliminating stored data. Unexpected or malicious clears corrupt the data flow and cause loss/corruption of sensitive queued transfers, so integrity is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: Raised by the FSM when an operation ends; triggers RX FIFO updates and returns FSM to IDLE.
Assets.Justification: serial.done gates operation retirement and FIFO update; if suppressed, transactions never complete and the FSM stays busy (stall), while spurious assertion retires partial slots or pushes invalid data, forcing retries and wedging the interface—both harming overall availability.

Assets.Functionality: Selects among the available external clock inputs (lowest 4 bits) for the internal clock generator, which derives the base tick (t_base) used to time 1-Wire operations.
Assets.Justification: If the chosen clock source or its values are tampered with, the base tick timing is altered, breaking protocol timing requirements and causing incorrect sampling or driving. Preserving its integrity is necessary to prevent corrupted 1-Wire transactions.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit write-data input whose fields (enable, prescaler, polarity, clock divider, duty) are sampled into the channel configuration registers on writes.
Assets.Justification: wdata_i carries the configuration values that become the channel's persistent configuration registers. If an attacker can alter wdata_i (or inject incorrect values via the bus path that drives it), the configuration fields (enable, prescaler, cdiv, duty, polarity) will be corrupted leading to incorrect PWM behavior.

Assets.Functionality: Write-enable input used to latch wdata_i into the channel configuration registers on the rising clock edge.
Assets.Justification: we_i controls when wdata_i is sampled into configuration registers; unauthorized toggling can cause unintended writes or race writes that corrupt configuration. Protecting the integrity of write gating is necessary to ensure register contents are not modified at incorrect times.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit duty-cycle configuration loaded from wdata_i(7 downto 0) that determines the compare threshold for the duty counter and shapes the PWM duty.
Assets.Justification: cfg_duty is the stored threshold that directly controls PWM on/off ratio; unauthorized modification corrupts the expected output waveform and changes device behavior. Integrity of this register is required so the PWM duty remains as configured by legitimate software.

Assets.Functionality: 10-bit fine clock divider loaded from wdata_i(17 downto 8) used as the terminal count for the fine divider (cnt_cdiv) to generate a single tick.
Assets.Justification: cfg_cdiv determines the frequency of cnt_tick events that drive the duty counter; corrupting cfg_cdiv changes PWM timing and may break timing guarantees. Thus cfg_cdiv must be protected from unauthorized modification to preserve correct timing behavior.

Assets.Functionality: 3-bit coarse prescaler select loaded from wdata_i(30 downto 28) that selects which bit of the clkgen_i vector is used as the pre-scaled clock source.
Assets.Justification: cfg_prsc selects which clkgen_i bit is used as the prescaled clock; altering it changes which clock source the channel uses and thus changes output frequency. Maintaining integrity of this selection prevents unintended frequency changes or misconfiguration.

Assets.Functionality: Per-channel select vector that indicates which channel is addressed by the current bus request (derived from bus address).
Assets.Justification: sel determines which channel receives configuration writes/reads; if sel is altered or corrupted, configuration operations may target the wrong channel and thus corrupt channel state. The selection logic integrity is therefore critical to prevent cross-channel configuration corruption.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit clock-divider input vector supplied by the global clock generator and forwarded to each channel to select pre-scaled clock bits used to generate ticks.
Assets.Justification: clkgen_i supplies the prescaled clock source bits used by channels to step their fine divider; if clkgen_i is unavailable or forced to values that never assert the selected bit, no cnt_tick events are generated and PWM activity halts. The absence or tampering of this input can therefore cause system-level denial-of-service of PWM outputs.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level enable signal that requests the global clock generator when any PWM channel requires clocking; asserted as the OR of per-channel requests.
Assets.Justification: clkgen_en_o is the module's request to the global clock generator; if this request cannot be propagated or is ignored, the global clock generator may not be enabled and channels will not receive the necessary clock source. Ensuring this signal's availability is necessary so the PWM subsystem can obtain clock resources and operate.

Assets.Functionality: Vector of PWM outputs (one bit per channel) aggregated from all instantiated channel controllers and presented to external logic.
Assets.Justification: pwm_o is the delivered functional output of the PWM controller; if pwm_o is blocked, forced, or otherwise made unavailable, the peripheral cannot perform its intended control/function (effectively a denial-of-service). The availability of pwm_o is therefore critical to the module's operational mission.

Assets.Functionality: External serial data line that is synchronized and sampled to be shifted into the receive shift register (serial.sreg).
Assets.Justification: Manipulating incoming data bits changes the bytes assembled into serial.sreg and thus the contents written to rx_fifo.wdata/rx_fifo on completion, directly corrupting payloads delivered to the CPU. This port is the direct attack point for altering received data values, so integrity is the dominant objective.

Assets.Functionality: Serial output driven from the MSB of the transmit shift register (serial.sreg) providing the transmitted bitstream to the external master.
Assets.Justification: If the output line is forced or otherwise prevented from toggling correctly at integration, remote receivers will not obtain correct transmit bits and the link is effectively broken. The port's availability is therefore critical for successful transmission to external devices.

Assets.Functionality: Derived edge-detection signal, generated by XORing clock history, that advances the serial FSM when clock edges are observed.
Assets.Justification: If sync.sck is lost or corrupted, the FSM cannot advance through bit phases. Without reliable edge detection, the serial engine stalls, leading to denial of service.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit shift register used for transmit (MSB drives sdi_dat_o) and to collect sampled bits for a received byte (written into RX FIFO when serial.done).
Assets.Justification: Corruption of serial.sreg changes both what is transmitted and what is captured as received data (and subsequently enqueued into RX FIFO), directly impacting data correctness end-to-end. Protecting the integrity of this register is therefore essential to prevent data corruption on the link.

Assets.Functionality: External low-active chip-select input. Its falling edge (after synchronization) starts a serial transfer and a high level aborts an ongoing transmission.
Assets.Justification: If CS is held inactive or manipulated at integration level, serial transfers never start (or are repeatedly aborted), effectively denying the peripheral's service. Because ctrl_cs_active and the serial FSM behavior are gated by this signal, CS is the primary attack point to stop normal operation.

Assets.Functionality: Asserts an interrupt to the CPU when the peripheral is enabled and configured FIFO/status conditions (RX/TX available, half/full, etc.) match enabled IRQ control bits.
Assets.Justification: If interrupts are suppressed, stuck, or incorrectly asserted at integration, the CPU may not be notified of FIFO conditions (or may be flooded with interrupts), causing missed servicing or unwanted preemption that impairs system operation. Timely/accurate interrupt signaling is therefore required for proper availability of the SDI service.

Assets.Functionality: Control bit written by the CPU to enable/disable the SDI; when '0' it causes tx_fifo and rx_fifo to be cleared and disables the serial engine (serial.state bit2 used).
Assets.Justification: Toggling this bit disables the entire peripheral and clears FIFOs, resulting in immediate service interruption and loss of queued data. Because it gates core operation and FIFO retention, it is the dominant availability control for the module.

Assets.Functionality: One-cycle pulse asserted at the beginning of a transmission to trigger a TX FIFO read (tx_fifo.re) and load transmit data into the shift register.
Assets.Justification: serial.start initiates each transfer and fetches the next byte from the TX FIFO; if suppressed the link never begins sending and stalls, while spurious pulses can double-pop or desynchronize the FIFO/shift register—both conditions impede forward progress of the SDI interface.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates whether the RX FIFO has free space (driven from rx_fifo.free) so upstream senders know whether they may push another RX beat.
Assets.Justification: If this signal is forced or manipulated to remain deasserted, upstream cannot send data and reception is stalled, producing a denial-of-service for incoming streams. The dominant impact is availability of the RX receive path.

Assets.Functionality: Indicates that a TX FIFO entry is available for transmission (driven from tx_fifo.avail) so the downstream can accept data when ready.
Assets.Justification: Suppressing or spurious assertion of this signal changes whether the downstream will attempt to consume data; forced deassertion prevents transmission (DoS), and spurious asserts may cause unexpected transfers. The main impact is availability of the TX service.

Assets.Functionality: Asserts when configured RX interrupt conditions are met (based on rx_fifo status bits and ctrl.irq_rx_* enables) while module is enabled; notifies the host of RX events.
Assets.Justification: Disabling or spoofing this interrupt prevents the host from being informed of RX data availability (or causes spurious interrupts), which can lead to missed processing or resource exhaustion; primary impact is availability/operational correctness.

Assets.Functionality: Asserted based on ctrl.enable and TX-side ctrl.irq_* settings combined with tx_fifo status to notify the host about TX conditions (empty/not-half/not-full).
Assets.Justification: Incorrect TX interrupt behavior (suppressed or spurious) can cause the host to miss transmit-ready conditions or to be overwhelmed by interrupts, impacting system responsiveness and service availability. The main concern is availability of the notification mechanism.

Assets.Functionality: Global enable flag from the control register; gates FIFO clears (rx_fifo.clear/tx_fifo.clear), enables interrupt generation and normal module operation.
Assets.Justification: Toggling this bit off causes RX/TX FIFOs to be cleared and disables normal operation (rx_fifo.clear <= not ctrl.enable), producing an immediate denial-of-service for both RX and TX flows. The dominant effect is availability of the entire SLINK functionality.

Assets.Functionality: Write-clear control that, when asserted, synchronously clears/flushes the RX FIFO (rx_fifo.clear). It is auto-clearing after write.
Assets.Justification: Asserting this control flushes received data and prevents consumption of previously queued RX items; unauthorized clearing is a denial-of-service on received data, so availability is the critical property.

Assets.Functionality: Write-clear control that, when asserted, synchronously clears/flushes the TX FIFO (tx_fifo.clear). It is auto-clearing after write.
Assets.Justification: Flushing the TX FIFO discards pending outgoing transfers and halts transmission until refilled, producing a DoS impact on outgoing streams; availability is the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: 32-bit TX output data presented from the TX FIFO read port when an entry is available for transmission to the downstream consumer.
Assets.Justification: This port carries the actual outgoing payload driven from the TX FIFO; any corruption of the data path or its source alters what is transmitted and therefore breaks data correctness. Integrity of transmitted payloads is the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: 4-bit destination information presented with TX data taken from the TX FIFO entry; used by downstream logic to route the outgoing beat.
Assets.Justification: If the destination tag is modified, outgoing data can be routed to the wrong consumer, violating correctness and possibly causing misdelivery. This is an integrity issue affecting routing of transmitted streams.

Assets.Functionality: Internal signal that stores the last-flag of the current RX FIFO read and is exposed through the control register (ctrl_rx_last_c) when the host reads status.
Assets.Justification: rx_last communicates framing state to the host. If modified, the host may misinterpret stream boundaries (e.g., thinking a stream ended when it did not), corrupting higher-level processing semantics.

Assets.Functionality: End-of-stream indicator for TX beats sourced from the TX FIFO entry; signals the last beat of a transmitted stream.
Assets.Justification: Incorrect last flags lead the downstream to mis-handle stream boundaries (e.g., truncation or concatenation), which is a correctness error in stream semantics. Preserving accurate end-of-stream marking is an integrity requirement.

Assets.Functionality: Configuration bits controlling SPI clock phase/polarity and prescaler/divider selection used by the clock_generator and transceiver to produce and sample SCK edges.
Assets.Justification: ctrl.prsc/cdiv set the SCK frequency and, with CPOL/CPHA, define drive/sample timing; if altered, SCK edges occur at the wrong rate or phase, violating setup/hold constraints and causing mis-sampling or framing errors that silently corrupt SPI transfers.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit shift register that holds the current transmit byte (MSB out) and collects sampled MISO bits during a transfer.
Assets.Justification: Any corruption of the shift register changes the bits transmitted on MOSI or the bits captured from MISO, directly altering exchanged data. Ensuring the correctness of this register during transfers is therefore an integrity concern.

Assets.Functionality: Serial clock output driven according to CPOL/CPHA and FSM phases to clock connected SPI peripherals.
Assets.Justification: If the clock output is blocked, stuck or disabled, peripherals cannot be clocked and all SPI data transfers stop, resulting in a clear denial-of-service. The primary impact of attacking this signal is preventing operation, so availability is dominant.

Assets.Functionality: Controller data out driven from the transmit shift register (MSB first) to send bits to the peripheral.
Assets.Justification: If MOSI is held, corrupted or prevented from toggling, peripherals will not receive intended commands/data and communication will fail. The foremost effect is denial-of-service to the peripheral link, making availability the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Array of active-low chip-select outputs controlled by CS control bits to select and enable a target SPI slave (one-hot addressing).
Assets.Justification: If CS lines are not asserted correctly (e.g., never driven low), the targeted peripheral will not be selected and transfers cannot proceed, causing service outage for that device. Thus availability of correct CS assertions is critical.

Assets.Functionality: Enable signal driven to an external clock generator to activate the prescaled clock source when the SPI is enabled.
Assets.Justification: If the external clock enable is prevented or deasserted, the prescaled clock input path will not produce the SPI timing source and transfers will stall. Its primary effect is preventing operation, making availability the dominant issue.

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt line asserted based on FIFO status and enabled IRQ conditions to notify the system of RX/TX/idle events when SPI is enabled.
Assets.Justification: Suppressing or spurious assertion of the IRQ line can prevent the system from responding to completed transfers or cause missed servicing, effectively denying timely event handling. Because this impacts receipt of notifications and workflow continuity, availability is the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Global enable bit that enables/disables the SPI controller; when deasserted it clears TX/RX FIFOs, gates clock generation and disables IRQs.
Assets.Justification: Toggling this bit disables the entire SPI datapath and clears buffers, which directly causes a denial-of-service for all SPI transfers and notifications. Because its primary effect is to make the SPI unusable when changed, availability is the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: A set of per-channel enables reduced by OR to form the internal gate signal 'en'. When 'en' is low, the divider counter is forced to zero and no clock-enable strobes are produced.
Assets.Justification: enable_i gates production of clock-enable strobes; if deasserted or glitched, 'en' stays low and the divider counter is held at zero so no strobes are emitted, stalling dependent logic. Spurious assertion/toggling can also disrupt timing by resetting/restarting the counters. Both cases directly impair forward progress, making availability the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: A 32-bit register holding the processor’s clock frequency, initialized from the generic CLOCK_FREQUENCY constant. It can also be modified at runtime by bus write operations to index 0 of the sysinfo array. Software reads this value through bus responses to obtain system timing and configuration data.
Assets.Justification: sysinfo(0) is the software-visible source of the CPU clock rate; if corrupted, drivers derive wrong divisors/timeouts (e.g., UART baud, timers, watchdog), causing mis-timed protocols, missed deadlines, or unsafe timing windows. Maintaining its correctness is essential to preserve system behavior and configuration integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Registered acknowledge for the SYSINFO peripheral: on each rising edge, buf_ack captures bus_req_i.stb and is then driven out as bus_rsp_o.ack; when buf_ack = '1', the module also returns the selected SYSINFO word on bus_rsp_o.data.
Assets.Justification: buf_ack is the liveness signal that completes SYSINFO read handshakes. Without a asserted acknowledge, requestors cannot retire the transaction and will wait indefinitely; with a spurious acknowledge, they may retire a transfer without receiving valid data. Because there is no alternate completion (error is not asserted), correct, timely assertion of buf_ack is required to maintain forward progress and overall system availability.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit random data byte produced by the neoTRNG core after de-biasing and LFSR-style mixing; at top level it is forwarded into the TRNG FIFO for host reads.
Assets.Justification: This signal carries the raw random byte produced by the entropy core before it is pushed to the FIFO. If observed or leaked, these bytes may be used as cryptographic secrets (keys/nonces) or to predict subsequent random values, so protecting confidentiality is essential.

Assets.Functionality: Single-cycle flag asserted by the neoTRNG core to indicate data_o contains a valid random byte; this signal is used as the FIFO write-enable so that completed random bytes are pushed into the random pool.
Assets.Justification: valid_o is the enqueue strobe for the random-pool FIFO; if suppressed, fresh bytes never enter the pool and consumers are starved, while spurious assertions enqueue stale/duplicate values and can jam flow control—both conditions reduce the availability of usable entropy.

Assets.Functionality: Single-bit synchronized output from each ring-oscillator entropy cell that is XOR-combined by the neoTRNG core to form the raw random stream prior to de-biasing and mixing.
Assets.Justification: Each rnd_o leaks the instantaneous state of a single entropy source; exposing or correlating these raw bits enables modeling or bias-extraction of individual cells and weakens unpredictability, so keeping them confidential is essential.

Assets.Functionality: On-chip FIFO (the 'random pool') that stores generated random bytes from neoTRNG until the host reads them via the bus interface; it exposes rdata to the bus read path and accepts wdata from the neoTRNG core.
Assets.Justification: The FIFO must deliver exactly the bytes produced by the entropy core in the correct order; any corruption, insertion, or loss of entries returns wrong data to software and undermines consumers that rely on untampered randomness.

Assets.Functionality: Synchronous clear signal for the random-pool FIFO that is auto-cleared and can be asserted via the control register write (ctrl_fifo_clr_c); also forces fifo.clear when enable = '0'.
Assets.Justification: An unexpected or malicious assertion of fifo_clr modifies (erases) the stored random-pool contents, corrupting the FIFO state and invalidating any expected data. This is fundamentally a data-integrity issue because it changes the stored values.

Assets.Functionality: Control bit and internal enable signal that starts and stops sampling: it gates the neoTRNG sampling state-machine / enable-shift-register chain and directly controls whether random data is produced and whether the FIFO is cleared when disabled.
Assets.Justification: If the enable path is stuck low or toggled maliciously, sampling halts and the FIFO may be cleared, denying random data to the system; conversely, inability to disable can prevent recovery/restart. Proper control of this signal is thus critical to availability.

Assets.Functionality: Status signal from the FIFO indicating whether data is available for bus reads; used when forming the control register read-back and to decide whether the data register should return stored bytes or zeros.
Assets.Justification: If fifo.avail is forced false or otherwise manipulated, the host will see no data available and cannot retrieve random bytes (reads return zeros). This results in denial of service for consumers of TRNG data, making availability the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: External I2C/Two-Wire data input line that is synchronized, filtered and sampled to detect start/stop conditions and to receive serial data bits into the bus engine.
Assets.Justification: If the SDA input is stuck, manipulated or not sampled correctly the module cannot detect start/stop or receive data bytes, preventing any transaction from progressing and causing a denial-of-service. As this module is not a crypto primitive, confidentiality is not the dominant concern; availability of the bus interface is primary.

Assets.Functionality: External I2C/Two-Wire clock input that is synchronized and edge-detected to time sampling and state-machine transitions for bit-level transfers.
Assets.Justification: SCL provides the timing basis for capturing and transmitting bits; if SCL is absent, held, or manipulated the engine cannot sample or progress through bytes, producing a denial-of-service on the peripheral. The primary impact is loss of operational availability rather than confidentiality.

Assets.Asset Name: Two-wire SDA output driver (ACK/NACK and data)
Assets.Functionality: Output driver used to pull the SDA line low for ACK/NACK and to transmit data bits during read operations; defaults to released/high when not driving.
Assets.Justification: twd_sda_o directly determines the bits placed on the bus (ACK/NACK and transmitted data). Tampering with this output or causing it to drive incorrect values changes the contents seen by the host or remote device, corrupting protocol exchanges and data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt signal asserted when enabled and configured conditions occur (RX data available, RX full, TX empty) to notify the CPU of peripheral events.
Assets.Justification: If interrupts are suppressed or blocked, the CPU may never be notified of available RX data or TX-empty conditions, preventing timely processing and effectively denying service. The primary risk is loss of functional responsiveness (DoS).

Assets.Functionality: Output enable signal to the SoC clock generator, asserted when the TWD module is enabled so that the selected sample clock signals (clkgen_i) are provided for input sampling.
Assets.Justification: This signal gates the sampling clocks required by the input synchronizer; if clock generation is inhibited (e.g., by forcing or suppressing the chain around this signal), the module's sampling/filtering stops and transactions cannot proceed, causing a denial-of-service.

Assets.Functionality: Top-level enable flag stored in the control register that turns the TWD module on/off; when '0' FIFOs are cleared, sampling is inactive and the module disables operation.
Assets.Justification: Changing ctrl.enable directly disables or enables all functional behavior (clears FIFOs, stops sampling and engine operation). An attacker or misconfiguration that forces the module disabled will prevent any peripheral operation, making availability the dominant concern.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit data output from the RX FIFO that is returned to the bus master on RX read accesses (the received bytes stored by the device).
Assets.Justification: rx_fifo.rdata is the definitive received-data value presented to the system; unauthorized modification corrupts the received information consumed by software, so data integrity of received bytes is the primary concern.

Assets.Functionality: Synchronous clear input to the RX FIFO instance, asserted when the module is disabled or when the ctrl.clr_rx control bit is written to clear stored RX data.
Assets.Justification: Clearing the RX FIFO discards received data and can prevent subsequent reads of those bytes; unauthorized or spurious assertion of this clear line leads to loss of data and denial of normal operation (DoS).

Assets.Functionality: Drives the I²C SDA line to assert START/STOP bits, data bits and ACK/NACK levels during transmissions (controller actively drives SDA low; otherwise line is released).
Assets.Justification: Incorrect SDA driving or release timing corrupts START/STOP edges, data bits, or ACK/NACK levels and can break arbitration—yielding malformed transactions and silent data corruption on the I²C bus.

Assets.Asset Name: TWI SDA Input (bus receiver / sampled SDA)
Assets.Functionality: Samples SDA to capture incoming bits and ACK/NACK from peripherals and supplies these samples to the serial engine which shifts them into engine.sreg and eventually into the RX FIFO.
Assets.Justification: If sampled SDA is corrupted or mis-synchronized, received bits and ACK/NACK are misinterpreted, producing wrong RX bytes and protocol errors—violating end-to-end data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: Controls selection of the pre-scaled input clock bit (prsc), fine clock division (cdiv) to create clk_gen.tick, and whether clock stretching is honored (clkstr), thus determining TWI timing and behavior.
Assets.Justification: These fields define SCL rate/phase and clock-stretch handling; tampering produces out-of-spec timing or ignores stretching, causing mis-sampling, framing errors, and corrupted transfers.

Assets.Functionality: Holds commands and data bytes (including dcmd fields) that the bus engine reads and executes to generate START/STOP and DATA transfers on the I²C bus.
Assets.Justification: Corruption of FIFO contents or strobes changes the command/data sequence (e.g., stray START/STOP, wrong bytes), leading to malformed bus transactions and incorrect device state.

Assets.Functionality: Generates the internal TWI timing pulses (based on prescaler and divider) used to step the phase generator and drive the engine for SCL/SDA phase transitions.
Assets.Justification: If clk_gen.tick does not occur (or is stalled), the engine will not progress through phases and no SCL pulses will be produced, effectively preventing any bus transactions and causing a denial-of-service of the TWI interface.

Assets.Functionality: Buffers received bytes (ACK+data) sampled by the engine and provides them to the host on read accesses when FIFO read is performed.
Assets.Justification: If entries are altered, lost, duplicated, or reordered, software reads corrupted payloads and makes wrong decisions; preserving RX FIFO contents is essential for data integrity.

Assets.Functionality: 8-bit pre-scaled clock vector from which a single bit (indexed via ctrl.prsc) is used as the input to the internal clock-divider/tick generator (affects clk_gen.tick timing).
Assets.Justification: clkgen_i is the timing source used to form clk_gen.tick; wrong tap selection or corrupted inputs shifts timing windows and breaks I²C setup/hold assumptions, corrupting transfers.

Assets.Asset Name: TWI SCL Input (clock sense / clock-stretch detection)
Assets.Functionality: Samples SCL to detect peripheral-driven clock-stretching and to sense bus state when the controller releases the line; sampled SCL contributes to clk_gen.halt assertion.
Assets.Justification: If SCL sampling is missing or incorrect, clock-stretch events are misdetected and the engine can stall waiting forever or advance prematurely—both conditions degrade bus availability.

Assets.Functionality: Global enable bit that activates/deactivates the TWI unit, controls clkgen_en_o and influences engine.state (when disabled the engine is offline and lines are released to pull-ups).
Assets.Justification: Toggling ctrl.enable disables the engine and clears FIFO state, preventing any TWI operations from occurring and causing immediate denial-of-service. Attackers or faulty writes to this control therefore directly stop the module from functioning at integration level.

Assets.Functionality: Interrupt line asserted when the module is enabled, the TX FIFO is empty and the bus engine is idle to notify the host that no pending transmissions remain.
Assets.Justification: If irq_o is not asserted (or is suppressed), the host may not be informed about completed transfers and may fail to enqueue new commands in a timely manner, causing stalled higher-level operation. Thus availability of the interrupt signal is important to maintain normal throughput and avoid a functional denial-of-service at integration level.

Assets.Functionality: Output driven from ctrl.enable that indicates whether the TWI internal clock generator should be enabled (used by surrounding logic to enable/disable clocking).
Assets.Justification: The external clock generator (or other system logic) may rely on this enable to start supplying the prescaled clock; if this signal is inactive or spoofed the downstream clocking may not be provided and the TWI subsystem will not operate. Therefore, its availability is critical to ensure the module can be clocked and function correctly in the integrated system.

Assets.Functionality: Serial transmit data output driven by the TX engine that emits start, data and stop bits onto the serial bus according to the transmit FSM and baud timing.
Assets.Justification: If uart_txd_o is blocked, corrupted or forced to an incorrect value at the integration boundary, external receivers will not receive transmitted bytes and the UART's transmit capability is effectively denied. The TX output is the observable communication channel for transmitted data, so its availability is critical to correct operation.

Assets.Functionality: Serial receive data input sampled and synchronized by the RX engine and written into the RX FIFO for CPU consumption.
Assets.Justification: If uart_rxd_i is held inactive, jittered, or otherwise made unavailable at the integration boundary, the receiver cannot recover incoming bytes and the UART cannot accept serial input. The receive physical line being available and correct is necessary for normal receive operation, so this I/O directly impacts availability.

Assets.Functionality: Hardware flow-control output that indicates whether the UART is ready to accept more incoming data (deasserted when RX FIFO half-full or UART disabled).
Assets.Justification: uart_rtsn_o is the mechanism the UART uses to throttle remote senders when local RX resources are constrained. If this signal is forced or otherwise misrepresented at the interface, remote peers may be prevented from sending or may overwhelm the RX FIFO, causing loss of service (DoS) or receive failures.

Assets.Functionality: Hardware flow-control input synchronized into the TX engine and used to gate transmission when hardware flow-control is enabled.
Assets.Justification: When HW flow-control is enabled, asserting CTS (or holding it asserted) prevents the TX engine from starting transmissions and can deny the ability to send data. Thus manipulation or unavailability of this input at integration-time can create a DoS on transmit functionality.

Assets.Functionality: Receive interrupt output asserted based on RX FIFO status and configured IRQ enables to notify the CPU about received data or FIFO thresholds.
Assets.Justification: If irq_rx_o is suppressed or blocked at integration, the host may not be promptly notified of incoming data which can prevent timely processing and cause buffering overflows or perceived unavailability of receive functionality. The interrupt output is therefore important for maintaining normal service availability.

Assets.Functionality: Transmit interrupt output asserted based on TX FIFO status and configured IRQ enables to notify the CPU that the TX FIFO is empty or below threshold.
Assets.Justification: If irq_tx_o is not delivered to the host, the system may not realize the TX FIFO needs refilling or that transmission resources are available, impairing throughput and possibly causing service interruptions. Thus this interrupt output is critical to maintaining normal transmit availability.

Assets.Functionality: Output driven by the UART enable control bit to gate/enable the external/internal clock generator used to produce the uart_clk timing signal.
Assets.Justification: Disabling or preventing the externally controlled clock domain (by manipulating this enable or the external generator) stops UART timing (transmit/receive), effectively denying all UART services. The enable is thus critical to the module's ability to operate.

Assets.Functionality: Control bit that enables/disables the UART. It drives clkgen_en_o, and is used to enable the transmitter and receiver state bits (tx_engine.state(2) and rx_engine.state(1)).
Assets.Justification: Unauthorized modification of ctrl.enable (e.g., toggling while engine is active) can alter behavior, clear state and corrupt ongoing transfers; it changes operational mode and can cause data loss or incorrect operation. Because it directly modifies the module's control state, its integrity is essential.

Assets.Functionality: Internal 8-bit bus carrying data written by the host into the TX FIFO to be enqueued for transmission.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or unauthorized modification of tx_fifo.wdata changes the bytes that will be transmitted, directly violating data integrity for outgoing data. As the internal representation of host-supplied transmit payloads, its integrity is required to preserve correct transmitted content.

Assets.Functionality: Control bit that enables or disables the watchdog; it gates the start of the timeout counter and drives the clock-generator enable output.
Assets.Justification: If this bit is modified by an attacker, the watchdog can be disabled (bypassed) or enabled unexpectedly, altering system protection semantics. The integrity of this control is essential to prevent unauthorized changes that would either remove the safety net (disable WDT) or change system behavior (enable WDT unexpectedly).

Assets.Functionality: Lock bit that prevents further writes to the control register when set; write attempts while locked trigger illegal-access handling.
Assets.Justification: Corruption or unauthorized modification of the lock bit allows attackers to change the WDT configuration (timeout/enable/strict) after lock was intended, breaking intended immutability. Maintaining lock integrity is necessary to ensure configured protection cannot be overridden by malicious writes.

Assets.Functionality: Bit that selects strict mode; when set, illegal accesses (wrong password or writes to a locked register) will trigger a hardware reset instead of being ignored.
Assets.Justification: Altering strict changes how the system reacts to illegal accesses and thus modifies system fault/response semantics; integrity is required to ensure the intended policy (tolerant vs. strict) is enforced. Unauthorized changes could either cause unexpected resets or suppress intended fault reactions.

Assets.Functionality: 24-bit programmed timeout loaded from the control register; compared against the internal counter to determine when a watchdog timeout occurs.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the timeout value can make the watchdog far too sensitive (causing spurious resets) or too lax (failing to reset when needed), directly undermining the WDT's protective role. Therefore the timeout field must maintain integrity to preserve correct timing behavior and system safety.

Assets.Functionality: Internal signal asserted when the timeout condition is met (cnt equals ctrl.timeout and prsc_tick) and the WDT is enabled; it contributes to driving rstn_o low.
Assets.Justification: This is the final path that generates a watchdog timeout reset; spurious assertion or manipulation resulting in unexpected resets (or suppression) directly impacts system availability.

Assets.Functionality: Two-bit register that records the cause of the last system reset (external, debugger, watchdog timeout, or invalid watchdog access) for readback.
Assets.Justification: Tampering with the reset-cause value can mislead diagnostics or monitoring logic about the true origin of resets, hiding malicious activity or confusing recovery procedures. The integrity of this register is important to ensure accurate system status and forensics.

Assets.Functionality: Output that enables an external clock generator when the watchdog is enabled; it is driven directly from the WDT enable control.
Assets.Justification: If this output is forced or disabled (e.g., via tampering at integration), the external clock generator can be turned off and downstream logic may lose clocking, causing denial-of-service. Availability of this output is critical because it controls whether parts of the system receive clocking from the external generator.

Assets.Functionality: Periodic tick derived from the external clock-generator input vector (clkgen_i) used to advance the watchdog counter on appropriate intervals.
Assets.Justification: If prsc_tick is absent, suppressed, or incorrectly produced the counter will not progress (or will progress incorrectly), preventing intended timeouts or causing erroneous timeouts and thus disrupting the WDT's availability/function.

Assets.Functionality: Internal control signal asserted when the correct password is written to the reset register; clears the timeout counter (i.e., 'feeds' the watchdog).
Assets.Justification: reset_wdt determines whether the watchdog is actually serviced; if suppressed despite a correct feed, the counter times out and forces unnecessary resets (DoS), while spurious assertion keeps the watchdog from ever expiring so hung software is never recovered—both directly harm system availability.
